Chapter 1 Strain

1.18 Do the strains fit together

In section 1.17 we computed from the displacement field of a body how the material is strained close to each point. When the partial derivatives of the displacements are small, this is described by six numbers, the components of the small strain tensor ((1.51)): three normal strains and three shear strains. Let us write them out once more:

\[\begin{aligned} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} &= \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} , & \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} &= \frac12\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x}\Big) , \\ \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} &= \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} , & \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} &= \frac12\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial z} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial x}\Big) , \\ \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} &= \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z} , & \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} &= \frac12\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial z} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial y}\Big) . \end{aligned} \tag{1.63}\]

Let us draw what these equations say. The left rectangle contains the three components of the displacement, \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\). The right rectangle contains the six components of the strain, two in a row. The blue arrow labelled \(\partial\) points from the left rectangle to the right one, because we get the strains from the displacements by differentiation according to (1.63). The grey dashed arrow with a question mark points back, because this is the opposite question of this section, which we cannot answer yet.

On the right-hand sides only three functions, the displacement components \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) appear, while on the left there are six. In this section we ask the opposite question. If six functions are given, is there a displacement field from which we get them by (1.63)? We will see that there is not always one. Six functions that come from three cannot be arbitrary: they must satisfy six equations. First, on the example of a strip, we look at how strains can fail to fit together. Then we meet derivatives of partial derivatives and show that for them the order in which we differentiate does not matter. With this we derive the six equations and say what they mean. Then we show that the strains determine the displacements up to a shift and a small rotation of the body. Finally we look at when the equations are enough for a displacement field to exist, and why they are not enough for a body with a hole.

1.18.1 Six functions from three

Why would anyone know the strains but not the displacements? In this chapter we always went from displacements to strains. In chapter 3, though, we will learn how the strain of a piece of material depends on the forces acting on it, and on whether it is heated. Then we will often know the strains before the displacements. In a body that is heated unevenly, for instance, every piece wants to stretch in its own way, as much as it was heated. If these stretches do not fit together, the pieces cannot stretch as they would like to, and they push on each other or pull on each other. So we must be able to check whether prescribed strains fit together.

For the bar this question did not come up. There the strain was a single function \(\varepsilon(x)\), and we get the displacement of a point by adding up the elongations of all pieces from the held end to the point (we will write this precisely in section 3.5). In space, though, three functions give six, and this is the reason why the six functions cannot be arbitrary.

What it means that strains do not fit together is easiest to picture like this (CM §3.7.1, PDF p. 149). Before loading we cut the body into small cubes. We strain each cube separately as the given strains prescribe, and then try to put the cubes back together into a whole body. If the strains are arbitrary, the cubes do not fit together without gaps or overlaps. They fit only if the strain of every cube agrees with the strains of its neighbours. In figure 1.380 the cubes are drawn as squares. For a strip cut into bands of squares we will see both in figure 1.383.

Let us try this on an example. A thin steel strip of length 200 mm and height 20 mm lies in a plane in which we place the axes \(x\) and \(y\) (figure 1.382). The axis \(x\) points along the strip, the axis \(y\) across it, and the origin is at the middle of the left end. So the strip reaches from \(x = 0\) to \(x = 200\) mm and from \(y = -10\) mm to \(y = 10\) mm. No force acts on it. This is a thought experiment: we prescribe a strain to every piece of the strip and ask whether the strip as a whole can take it. Let us prescribe

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = k\,y^2 , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0 , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0 , \tag{1.64}\]

and let the other three components be zero. The number \(k\) is a constant. Since \(y^2\) has the unit m² and a strain has no unit, \(k\) has the unit m⁻². Let us take \(k = -10\) m⁻², so that the strains at the edges are a thousandth in size, which by section 1.1 is the upper limit for the strains of steel structures. The longitudinal fibre in the middle of the strip, where \(y = 0\), is to keep its length. The longitudinal fibres at the edges, where \(y = \pm 10\) mm, are to shorten by \(10\ \text{m}^{-2} \cdot (0{,}01\ \text{m})^2 = 0{,}001\), by a thousandth. The fibres at the height \(y = \pm 5\) mm are to shorten by \(10\ \text{m}^{-2} \cdot (0{,}005\ \text{m})^2 = 0{,}00025\), four times less, because \(y\) is half as large there and so \(y^2\) is four times smaller. The prescribed strains of the five fibres drawn in figure 1.382 are therefore:

height \(y\) \(-10\) mm \(-5\) mm \(0\) \(5\) mm \(10\) mm
\(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = k\,y^2\) \(-0{,}001\) \(-0{,}00025\) \(0\) \(-0{,}00025\) \(-0{,}001\)

Let us draw this as we would on a board. On the left is the blackwhite rectangle, the strip before deformation, with five horizontal lines, which are the longitudinal fibres at the heights \(-10\), \(-5\), \(0\), \(5\) and \(10\) mm. The strip is drawn proportionally shorter and taller than in reality, so that it can be drawn. The axis \(x\) points along the strip, the axis \(y\) across it. The heights of the fibres in millimetres are written at their left ends. We then draw each fibre also after the deformation, in orange, from the same left end. A short transverse tick marks the end of the shortened fibre, and the blackwhite remainder shows by how much it has shortened. The fibre in the middle does not shorten, so the orange line reaches the right edge. The fibres at \(y = \pm 5\) mm shorten by \(0{,}00025\), the fibres at the edges by \(0{,}001\). The shortening is greatly magnified in the figure: at the edges it is drawn as a quarter of the length instead of a thousandth, so that it can be seen. So the differences between the fibres are visible, although in reality they are tiny.

On the right is the graph of the strain. The horizontal axis is \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), the vertical one is the height \(y\) with the same scale as the strip, so the fibres and the points of the graph are at the same height. The labels on the vertical axis are heights in millimetres. The blue parabola is the prescribed strain \(k\,y^2\). Its vertex is at \(y = 0\), because the strain is zero there, and it opens to the left, because \(k\) is negative. On it are the five blue dots, the values of the five fibres from the table. The horizontal grey dashed lines lead from the dots to the axis \(y\), so that it can be seen at which height each dot lies. The vertical grey dashed lines lead from the dots down to the values below the graph, \(-0{,}001\) at \(y = \pm 10\) mm and \(-0{,}00025\) at \(y = \pm 5\) mm.

Let us look at a small piece of the strip at the top edge. The blackwhite piece is before the deformation, \(\Delta x\) long and \(\Delta y\) high. The orange piece is after the deformation. The longitudinal sides are shorter, because \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} < 0\). The transverse sides keep the length \(\Delta y\), because \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0\), and the right angles between longitudinal and transverse sides stay right, because \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\). The shortening is greatly enlarged in the figure.

Do the pieces strained in this way fit together into a strip? Let us draw what we will do. The blackwhite grid on the left is the strip before deformation, cut into five horizontal bands of five squares. The axis \(x\) points along the bands, the axis \(y\) upwards. The deformation is greatly magnified in the figure, so that it can be seen. In the middle the strip is drawn in orange with every band deformed by \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = y/R\), and on the right in orange the strip with every band deformed by \(k\,y^2\). The grey shapes between the bands on the right are gaps that open where the bands do not touch. We strained each band of the right strip as (1.64) prescribes at the heights that the band covers, and we placed all the bands one on top of another at the left end, so that they touch there. The band is 4 mm high, so the strain changes also within the band. For the band between \(y = 2\) mm and \(y = 6\) mm the upper edge shortens by \(10\ \text{m}^{-2} \cdot (0{,}006\ \text{m})^2 = 0{,}00036\), and the lower edge by only \(10\ \text{m}^{-2} \cdot (0{,}002\ \text{m})^2 = 0{,}00004\). The shorter upper edge bends the band upward. Why the band curves in this way, figure 1.392 in section 1.18.3 shows exactly. The band in the middle stays straight, because its edges at \(y = \pm 2\) mm shorten equally. The bands above it curve upward, the bands below it downward, and the farther from the middle a band lies, the more it curves. So gaps open between the bands, and they get wider and wider towards the right end. The pieces do not fit together.

For comparison, figure 1.383 in the middle shows the same strip with the prescribed strain

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \frac{y}{R} , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0 , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0 , \qquad R = 10\ \text{m} ,\]

and the other components zero. The longitudinal fibres above the middle get longer and those below it shorter, in proportion to the distance from the middle, at the edges by a thousandth, since \(0{,}01\ \text{m} / 10\ \text{m} = 0{,}001\). Here all bands curve in the same way, like parts of rings around the same centre, and they fit together without gaps. A bent horizontal bar, which we will treat in chapter 5, curves in a similar way.

For the second strip a displacement field exists. We find it by guessing and checking. The function \(x\,y/R\) has the derivative \(y/R\) with respect to \(x\), so let us take \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = x\,y/R\). Its derivative with respect to \(y\) is \(x/R\), and for the shear to be zero we need \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x = -x/R\). The function \(-x^2/(2R)\) has such a derivative, and it does not depend on \(y\), as \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0\) requires. So the field is

\[u_{\mathrm{x}} = \frac{x\,y}{R} , \qquad u_{\mathrm{y}} = -\frac{x^2}{2R} , \qquad u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0 .\]

Let us check it with (1.63). We compute partial derivatives as ordinary derivatives in which the other variables are treated as numbers, with the rules of lemma 1.81 on the rules of differentiation.

  1. In \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial x\) the factor \(y/R\) is a constant, and the derivative of \(x\) with respect to \(x\) is \(1\), so \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = y/R\).
  2. The component \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) does not depend on \(y\), so \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial y = 0\).
  3. We have \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial y = x/R\) and \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x = -2x/(2R) = -x/R\). The sum is zero, so \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = \tfrac12\,(x/R - x/R) = 0\).
  4. The component \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) is zero, and \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) do not depend on \(z\), so \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\) are zero.

The component \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = -x^2/(2R)\) does not depend on the height \(y\). So all longitudinal fibres curve into the same shape, and that is exactly why the bands fit together (figure 1.383, middle). The right end of the strip at \(x = 0{,}2\) m drops by \(0{,}2^2/(2 \cdot 10)\ \text{m} = 0{,}002\) m, by 2 mm.

For the first strip, though, we will not find such a field. Before we show this, let us write down precisely what we are looking for.

Definition 1.123 Compatible strains (kompatibilne deformacije)

Let \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\) be functions of three variables defined at the interior points of a body. These functions are compatible strains (kompatibilne deformacije) if there is a continuously differentiable displacement field \(\vek u = (u_{\mathrm{x}}, u_{\mathrm{y}}, u_{\mathrm{z}})\) (definition 1.90), defined at the same points, such that the equations (1.63) hold at each of them.

Source: BARBER §2.2.1 (PDF p. 46), CM §3.7.1 (PDF p. 149).

The word compatibility means the ability to go together: strains are compatible if the strained pieces go together into a whole body. By definition 1.23 a displacement field assigns to every point a single displacement vector. This matters: pieces that do not fit together would mean that the same point had to get two different displacements, one as part of one piece and another as part of its neighbour. The strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = y/R\) are compatible, since we found a displacement field for them. For the strains (1.64) we will show in section 1.18.3 that they are not.

Why do the bands of the first strip curve differently (figure 1.383, right)? The longitudinal fibres at different heights shorten differently, and we will see that this makes the strip curve, and the faster the strain changes with height, the more strongly it curves. To write this precisely we need the derivative of a partial derivative and the fact that it does not matter in which order we differentiate twice.

1.18.2 Second partial derivatives

Let us return to the hanging bar. A steel bar of length \(L = 10\) m with a diameter of 10 mm hangs and stretches under its own weight. It is held in an idealized way: only the point \(O\) at the centre of the top end is fixed, and the weight is carried by a force spread evenly over the top face. The axis \(x\) points from \(O\) vertically down, the axes \(y\) and \(z\) lie horizontally. By (1.18) the displacement field is

\[\begin{aligned} u_{\mathrm{x}}(x, y, z) &= a\,(2Lx - x^2) - 0{,}3\,a\,(y^2 + z^2) , \\ u_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y, z) &= -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,y , \\ u_{\mathrm{z}}(x, y, z) &= -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,z , \qquad a = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1} . \end{aligned}\]

We will look mainly at the component \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\), the displacement in the direction of the axis \(y\). By the table in section 1.7.2 its partial derivatives with respect to \(y\) and to \(x\) are

\[\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y}(x, y, z) = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x) , \qquad \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x}(x, y, z) = 0{,}6\,a\,y .\]

Let us draw the bar, seen from the side. The blackwhite rectangle is the bar before loading. The hatched line above it is the ceiling that carries the bar. The top face is not glued to it. It is carried by a distributed force, which is not drawn, so the face can narrow. The blackwhite dot on it is the fixed point \(O\). The arrow to the left of the bar shows the direction of the axis \(x\). The axis itself goes through \(O\), it is drawn at the side so that it does not cover the bar. The orange line is the outline of the bar after loading. At the top the bar is narrower than at the bottom, because \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,y\) is larger in size at smaller \(x\) and is negative at \(y > 0\): the right edge moves towards the axis, and the left edge equally towards the axis from the other side. The narrowing is greatly magnified. In reality the bar at the top gets thinner by only \(0{,}6\,a\,L = 1{,}17 \cdot 10^{-6}\) of its radius, while in the figure it is \(0{,}3\) of the radius, so it is magnified about \(256\,000\) times. We measure the displacement of the right edge at two depths. The grey dimension on the left is the depth \(x\) from the top end, the second grey dimension is the depth \(x + \Delta x\). At each depth the blue arrow shows the displacement \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) of the edge. The arrow is short, so a grey dashed line at the same height leads from it to the blue label \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) on the right. The upper arrow is longer than the lower one, because the narrowing is larger at the top.

In section 1.7.3 we saw that the slope \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial y\) at the depth \(x + \Delta x\) is slightly different from that at the depth \(x\), because lower down the bar thins less (figure 1.104). In figure 1.384 we see the slope as the displacement of the right edge. At constant \(x\) the displacement \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) is proportional to \(y\), so the displacement of an edge 5 mm from the axis equals the slope multiplied by 5 mm. The displacement \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) at the depth \(x\) is therefore larger in size than the displacement at the depth \(x + \Delta x\). So a partial derivative is again a function of the point, and we can ask how fast it changes as we move. This is a derivative of a derivative.

Let us draw two graphs. On the left, the horizontal axis is the depth \(x\), from the top end to the end of the bar at \(L\), and the vertical axis is the derivative \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial y\). The blackwhite line is this derivative. At \(x = 0\) it has the value \(-0{,}6\,a\,L\), and at \(x = L\) zero, because \(L - x = 0\) there. It is a line because \(-0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\) is a linear function. The blue triangle on the left measures the slope of this line. The horizontal leg is the step \(\Delta x\), and the vertical one is the change of the derivative over this step, \(0{,}6\,a\,\Delta x\). The slope is their quotient, \(0{,}6\,a\). On the right graph the horizontal axis is the coordinate \(y\), measured from the axis of the bar, so it runs into negative values too, and the vertical axis is the derivative \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x\). The blackwhite line goes through the origin, because \(0{,}6\,a\,y\) is proportional to \(y\). The blue triangle again measures the slope. Its horizontal leg is \(\Delta y\), the vertical one \(0{,}6\,a\,\Delta y\), and the quotient is again \(0{,}6\,a\). The graphs have different scales on the two axes. On the left graph the length of the bar, 10 m, is drawn horizontally, and on the right graph its diameter, 10 mm, over the same length. So the lines do not look equally steep, although both slopes are equal to \(0{,}6\,a\) when \(x\) and \(y\) are measured in the same unit.

Let us compute how fast \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial y\) changes with depth. In figure 1.385 this is the slope of the left graph. We split the expression \(-0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\) into \(-0{,}6\,a\,L + 0{,}6\,a\,x\). The first term is a constant, with derivative zero, and by lemma 1.81 on the rules of differentiation the second has the derivative \(0{,}6\,a\). So

\[\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y}\Big) = 0{,}6\,a = 1{,}171 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1} .\]

When we go down by 1 m, the slope \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial y\) grows by \(1{,}171 \cdot 10^{-7}\). Since it is negative, its size decreases: lower down the bar thins less.

Definition 1.124 Second partial derivatives (drugi parcialni odvodi)

Let \(f\) be a function of three variables, and let its partial derivative \(\partial f / \partial x\) exist at all points whose distance from the point \(P\) is less than some number \(r > 0\). Then \(\partial f / \partial x\) is again a function of three variables, defined at these points. Its partial derivative with respect to \(y\) at the point \(P\), if it exists, is the second partial derivative (drugi parcialni odvod) of the function \(f\), first with respect to \(x\) and then with respect to \(y\):

\[\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\,\partial x}(P) = \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\Big(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\Big)(P) . \tag{1.65}\]

In the same way we define the second partial derivative for every pair of variables from \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\), also for a pair of equal variables, which we write \(\partial^2 f / \partial x^2\). A second partial derivative with respect to two different variables is a mixed partial derivative (mešani odvod). Partial derivatives of third order are obtained in the same way from second partial derivatives, for example

\[\frac{\partial^3 f}{\partial z\,\partial y\,\partial x}(P) = \frac{\partial}{\partial z}\Big(\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\,\partial x}\Big)(P) .\]

Source: LEBL2 §8.6 (PDF p. 60), for functions of \(n\) variables and derivatives of any order.

Let us draw the chain of differentiation. The top row starts at the function \(f\). The first blue arrow labelled \(\partial / \partial x\) means differentiation with respect to \(x\) and leads to the derivative \(\partial f / \partial x\). The second blue arrow means differentiation with respect to \(y\) and leads to the second derivative. In the bottom row we start at the same function \(f\), differentiate first with respect to \(y\) to \(\partial f / \partial y\) and then with respect to \(x\) to the second derivative. The top chain is blue, because its result is the derivative \(\partial^2 f / \partial y\,\partial x\) from definition 1.124. The bottom chain is blackwhite and has the opposite order. Between the results stands the sign \(= ?\), because we do not yet know whether they are equal.

A second partial derivative at a point is a number. As a function of the point it is again a function of three variables, which we can differentiate further. A function of three variables has nine second partial derivatives, one for each of the nine choices of the first and the second variable. The notation \(\partial^2 f / \partial y\,\partial x\) is read from right to left: first we differentiate with respect to the variable standing closest to \(f\), that is \(x\), and then with respect to \(y\). Some books write a mixed derivative with subscripts, \(f_{\mathrm{xy}}\), and then the subscripts stand in the opposite order to our notation (LEBL2, PDF p. 60). As with partial derivatives, we do not use subscripts. The condition that \(\partial f / \partial x\) exists at all points near \(P\) is needed because the definition of the partial derivative 1.25 needs the function \(\partial f / \partial x\) at the points \((x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}} + \Delta y, z_{\mathrm{P}})\) for all small enough \(\Delta y\).

For the hanging bar we computed above the mixed derivative \(\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x\,\partial y = 0{,}6\,a\). Let us compute the other second partial derivatives of the component \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) too. The derivative in a row is the first derivative, and the column says with respect to which variable we differentiate it the second time. Differentiating \(0{,}6\,a\,y\) with respect to \(y\) gives \(0{,}6\,a\), and with respect to \(x\) and to \(z\) zero, because \(x\) and \(z\) do not appear in the expression. The derivative of \(-0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\) with respect to \(x\) we computed above, and with respect to \(y\) and to \(z\) it is zero. The derivative \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial z\) is zero at every point, so all its derivatives are zero as well.

w.r.t. \(x\) w.r.t. \(y\) w.r.t. \(z\)
\(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x = 0{,}6\,a\,y\) \(0\) \(0{,}6\,a\) \(0\)
\(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial y = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\) \(0{,}6\,a\) \(0\) \(0\)
\(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial z = 0\) \(0\) \(0\) \(0\)

The two mixed derivatives with respect to \(x\) and \(y\) are equal (figure 1.385):

\[\frac{\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y\,\partial x} = \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\big(0{,}6\,a\,y\big) = 0{,}6\,a , \qquad \frac{\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x\,\partial y} = \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\big(-0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\big) = 0{,}6\,a .\]

We read the meaning of both in two steps, first the meaning of the first derivative, then the meaning of its derivative:

  • The first derivative \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x = 0{,}6\,a\,y\) says how fast the displacement toward the axis decreases as we go down. This rate is larger the farther from the axis we are (right graph). The mixed derivative \(\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial y\,\partial x = 0{,}6\,a\) says by how much this rate grows per metre of distance from the axis (slope of the right graph).
  • The first derivative \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial y = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\) says how strongly the bar thins at the depth \(x\) (left graph). The mixed derivative \(\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x\,\partial y = 0{,}6\,a\) says by how much this thinning decreases per metre of depth (slope of the left graph).

So the first mixed derivative measures how the rate of decrease of the displacement changes with the distance from the axis, and the second how the thinning changes with depth. These two changes sound different, yet they are equal. For the components \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\), too, the two mixed derivatives are equal for every pair of variables. For \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\), for example, \(\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial y\,\partial x = \partial / \partial y\,\big(2a\,(L - x)\big) = 0\) and \(\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial x\,\partial y = \partial / \partial x\,(-0{,}6\,a\,y) = 0\).

Is the equality a coincidence? Let us look at four values of a function \(f\) at the corners of a small rectangle whose sides are parallel to the axes \(x\) and \(y\) (figure 1.387). Let the coordinate \(z\) be \(z_{\mathrm{P}}\) everywhere, so we leave it out of the notation and write \(f(x, y)\) instead of \(f(x, y, z_{\mathrm{P}})\). The corners are \((x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}})\), \((x_{\mathrm{P}} + s, y_{\mathrm{P}})\), \((x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}} + t)\) and \((x_{\mathrm{P}} + s, y_{\mathrm{P}} + t)\), where \(s\) and \(t\) are positive numbers. We add the values with alternating signs:

\[\begin{aligned} g(s, t) &= f(x_{\mathrm{P}} + s, y_{\mathrm{P}} + t) - f(x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}} + t) \\ &\quad - f(x_{\mathrm{P}} + s, y_{\mathrm{P}}) + f(x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}}) . \end{aligned} \tag{1.66}\]

We call the number \(g(s, t)\) the double difference. Let us draw it. The axis \(x\) points to the right, the axis \(y\) up. The rectangle has the side \(s\) along \(x\) and the side \(t\) along \(y\). Its four corners are the points at which we take the values of \(f\). The bottom left corner is the point \(P\). The grey dashed lines and the labels on the axes show the coordinates of the corners: \(x_{\mathrm{P}}\) and \(x_{\mathrm{P}} + s\) on the axis \(x\), \(y_{\mathrm{P}}\) and \(y_{\mathrm{P}} + t\) on the axis \(y\). The signs beside the corners belong to the values in the equation: plus at \((x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}})\) and \((x_{\mathrm{P}} + s, y_{\mathrm{P}} + t)\), minus at the other two. Two blue arrows outside the top and bottom sides point in the direction of the axis \(x\), because there we will look at the change of \(f\) along \(x\). Two blackwhite arrows outside the right and left sides point in the direction of the axis \(y\) for the same reason. Inside the rectangle are two points that the proof below will find. The blue point \(Q_1\) lies on the horizontal grey dashed line at the height \(y_{\mathrm{P}} + t_1\). It is blue because the proof finds it from the changes along the blue arrows. The blackwhite point \(Q_2\) lies on the vertical grey dashed line at \(x_{\mathrm{P}} + s_2\) and the proof finds it from the changes along the blackwhite arrows. What the numbers \(t_1\) and \(s_2\) are, we say in the proof, the drawn positions of the points are only an example. We can group the terms in two ways.

  1. The first two and the last two: \(\big(f(x_{\mathrm{P}} + s, y_{\mathrm{P}} + t) - f(x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}} + t)\big) - \big(f(x_{\mathrm{P}} + s, y_{\mathrm{P}}) - f(x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}})\big)\). This is the change of \(f\) along the top side, in the direction of the axis \(x\), minus the change along the bottom side (blue arrows in figure 1.387). Divided by \(s\), it gives approximately \(\partial f / \partial x\) at the height \(y_{\mathrm{P}} + t\) minus \(\partial f / \partial x\) at the height \(y_{\mathrm{P}}\). Divided further by \(t\), it gives approximately how fast \(\partial f / \partial x\) changes with \(y\), that is \(\partial^2 f / \partial y\,\partial x\).
  2. The first and the third, and the second and the fourth: \(\big(f(x_{\mathrm{P}} + s, y_{\mathrm{P}} + t) - f(x_{\mathrm{P}} + s, y_{\mathrm{P}})\big) - \big(f(x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}} + t) - f(x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}})\big)\). This is the change along the right side, in the direction of the axis \(y\), minus the change along the left side (blackwhite arrows). Divided by \(t\) and by \(s\), it is approximately \(\partial^2 f / \partial x\,\partial y\).

So the same number \(g(s, t)/(s\,t)\) approximates both mixed derivatives (the changes along the sides of the rectangle), and we expect them to be equal. For the component \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,y\) of the hanging bar, which does not depend on \(z\), the double difference is

\[\begin{aligned} g(s, t) &= -0{,}6\,a\,\big[(L - x_{\mathrm{P}} - s)(y_{\mathrm{P}} + t) - (L - x_{\mathrm{P}})(y_{\mathrm{P}} + t) \\ &\qquad - (L - x_{\mathrm{P}} - s)\,y_{\mathrm{P}} + (L - x_{\mathrm{P}})\,y_{\mathrm{P}}\big] . \end{aligned}\]

In the square bracket the first two terms together give \(-s\,(y_{\mathrm{P}} + t)\), and the last two give \(s\,y_{\mathrm{P}}\). The sum is \(-s\,t\), so \(g(s, t) = 0{,}6\,a\,s\,t\) and \(g(s, t)/(s\,t) = 0{,}6\,a\) for all \(s\) and \(t\), exactly the two mixed derivatives. For a general function, though, the quotient \(g(s, t)/(s\,t)\) need not equal either of the mixed derivatives at \(P\). With the mean value theorem 1.84, used twice, we show that it equals a mixed derivative at some point inside the rectangle. As the rectangle shrinks, this point approaches \(P\), and if the mixed derivative is continuous, its value approaches the value at \(P\).

Theorem 1.125 Symmetry of mixed partial derivatives (zamenljivost mešanih odvodov)

Let \(f\) be a function of three variables defined at all points whose distance from the point \(P = (x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}}, z_{\mathrm{P}})\) is less than some number \(r > 0\). Let the partial derivatives \(\partial f / \partial x\) and \(\partial f / \partial y\) and the mixed derivatives \(\partial^2 f / \partial y\,\partial x\) and \(\partial^2 f / \partial x\,\partial y\) exist at all these points, and let the two mixed derivatives be continuous at the point \(P\) (definition 1.67). Then

\[\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\,\partial x}(P) = \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\,\partial y}(P) . \tag{1.67}\]

The same holds for the variables \(x\) and \(z\) and for the variables \(y\) and \(z\).

Proof

We must show that the two mixed derivatives at \(P\) are the same number. Throughout the proof the coordinate \(z\) equals \(z_{\mathrm{P}}\), so we leave it out of the notation: \(f(x, y)\) means \(f(x, y, z_{\mathrm{P}})\), and likewise for the partial derivatives.

  1. We pick positive numbers \(s\) and \(t\) with \(s^2 + t^2 < r^2\). Every point \((x_{\mathrm{P}} + v, y_{\mathrm{P}} + w)\) with \(0 \le v \le s\) and \(0 \le w \le t\) is at the distance \(\sqrt{v^2 + w^2} \le \sqrt{s^2 + t^2} < r\) from \(P\) ((1.10)). So the rectangle with the corners \((x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}})\) and \((x_{\mathrm{P}} + s, y_{\mathrm{P}} + t)\) lies entirely among the points at which, by assumption, we know all the derivatives used. Let \(g(s, t)\) be the double difference (1.66).
  2. For numbers \(v\) between \(0\) and \(t\) we define the function of one variable \(\varphi_1(v) = f(x_{\mathrm{P}} + s, y_{\mathrm{P}} + v) - f(x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}} + v)\). This is the change of \(f\) in the direction of the axis \(x\) at the height \(y_{\mathrm{P}} + v\). Putting in \(v = t\) and \(v = 0\) we get \(\varphi_1(t) - \varphi_1(0) = g(s, t)\), since these are exactly the four terms of (1.66). The value \(\varphi_1(t)\) is the change along the top side, and \(\varphi_1(0)\) the change along the bottom side.
  3. Each of the two terms of \(\varphi_1\) is the function \(f\) along a line in the direction of the axis \(y\). Its derivative with respect to \(v\) is, by the definition of the partial derivative 1.25, the partial derivative \(\partial f / \partial y\), which exists by assumption. The derivative of a difference is the difference of the derivatives (lemma 1.81 on the rules of differentiation), so \(\varphi_1\) has a derivative at every point of the interval \([0, t]\), a one-sided one at the end points (definition 1.9). We need the derivative at the end points \(v = 0\) and \(v = t\) so that \(\varphi_1\) is continuous at the end points too, which the mean value theorem in step 4 requires. It exists because the inequality \(\sqrt{s^2 + t^2} < r\) is strict. The points just below the bottom side and just above the top side are still closer to \(P\) than \(r\), so \(\partial f / \partial y\) exists at the corners too, as a limit of the difference quotient from both sides. When the limit from both sides exists, the limit from one side only exists too and is equal to it (section 1.3.3). At every point of the interval \([0, t]\) therefore
    \[\varphi_1'(v) = \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_{\mathrm{P}} + s, y_{\mathrm{P}} + v) - \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}} + v) .\]
    By lemma 1.79, that a differentiable function is continuous, \(\varphi_1\) is continuous on the interval \([0, t]\).
  4. By the mean value theorem 1.84 there is a number \(t_1\) between \(0\) and \(t\) such that \(\varphi_1(t) - \varphi_1(0) = \varphi_1'(t_1)\,t\). In the figure this is the height \(y_{\mathrm{P}} + t_1\). By steps 2 and 3, therefore,
    \[g(s, t) = t\,\Big(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_{\mathrm{P}} + s, y_{\mathrm{P}} + t_1) - \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}} + t_1)\Big) .\]
  5. For numbers \(w\) between \(0\) and \(s\) we define \(\psi_1(w) = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_{\mathrm{P}} + w, y_{\mathrm{P}} + t_1)\). The bracket of step 4 is \(\psi_1(s) - \psi_1(0)\). The function \(\psi_1\) is the function \(\partial f / \partial y\) along the horizontal segment at the height \(y_{\mathrm{P}} + t_1\). Its derivative with respect to \(w\) is, by the definition of second partial derivatives 1.124, the mixed derivative \(\partial^2 f / \partial x\,\partial y\), which exists by assumption, so \(\psi_1\) is differentiable at every point of the interval \([0, s]\), one-sidedly at the end points, since the mixed derivative exists there as a limit on both sides, as in step 3. So by lemma 1.79 it is continuous on \([0, s]\).
  6. By the mean value theorem there is a number \(s_1\) between \(0\) and \(s\) such that \(\psi_1(s) - \psi_1(0) = \psi_1'(s_1)\,s\). Let \(Q_1 = (x_{\mathrm{P}} + s_1, y_{\mathrm{P}} + t_1)\). With step 4 we get
    \[g(s, t) = s\,t\,\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\,\partial y}(Q_1) .\]
  7. We proceed in the same way with the roles of \(x\) and \(y\) swapped. For numbers \(w\) between \(0\) and \(s\) let \(\varphi_2(w) = f(x_{\mathrm{P}} + w, y_{\mathrm{P}} + t) - f(x_{\mathrm{P}} + w, y_{\mathrm{P}})\), the change in the direction of the axis \(y\) at the place \(x_{\mathrm{P}} + w\). For it, too, \(\varphi_2(s) - \varphi_2(0) = g(s, t)\), where \(\varphi_2(s)\) is the change along the right side and \(\varphi_2(0)\) the change along the left side. Steps 3 to 6 with the variables swapped give a number \(s_2\) between \(0\) and \(s\), a number \(t_2\) between \(0\) and \(t\) and the point \(Q_2 = (x_{\mathrm{P}} + s_2, y_{\mathrm{P}} + t_2)\) on the vertical segment at \(x_{\mathrm{P}} + s_2\) such that
    \[g(s, t) = s\,t\,\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\,\partial x}(Q_2) .\]
  8. The right-hand sides of steps 6 and 7 are equal, because both equal \(g(s, t)\). We divide them by \(s\,t \neq 0\) and get that the mixed derivative at \(Q_1\) equals the mixed derivative at \(Q_2\):
    \[\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\,\partial y}(Q_1) = \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\,\partial x}(Q_2) .\]
  9. Now we use continuity. In figure 1.388 on the right, on the number line, \(m_1\) is the mixed derivative \(\partial^2 f / \partial x\,\partial y\,(P)\) and \(m_2\) is the mixed derivative \(\partial^2 f / \partial y\,\partial x\,(P)\), which we compare. We pick any error \(\eta > 0\). Since \(\partial^2 f / \partial x\,\partial y\) is continuous at \(P\), for the error \(\eta/2\) there is a \(\delta_1 > 0\) such that the value at every point whose distance from \(P\) is less than \(\delta_1\) differs from the value at \(P\) by less than \(\eta/2\) (the blue interval around \(m_1\)). Likewise, for \(\partial^2 f / \partial y\,\partial x\) there is a \(\delta_2 > 0\).
  10. Let \(\rho\) be the smallest of the numbers \(\delta_1\), \(\delta_2\) and \(r\), and take \(s = t = \rho/2\). In the figure there is the ball of radius \(\rho\) around \(P\), and in it the rectangle with the sides \(s\) and \(t\). Then \(s^2 + t^2 = \rho^2/2 < r^2\), so step 1 applies. The points \(Q_1\) and \(Q_2\) are at a distance less than \(\sqrt{s^2 + t^2} = \rho/\sqrt 2 < \rho\) from \(P\), since their coordinates lie strictly between the coordinates of the corners. Therefore
    \[\Big|\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\,\partial y}(P) - \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\,\partial y}(Q_1)\Big| < \frac{\eta}{2} , \qquad \Big|\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\,\partial x}(Q_2) - \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\,\partial x}(P)\Big| < \frac{\eta}{2} .\]
  11. By step 8 the mixed derivatives at \(Q_1\) and \(Q_2\) have a common value \(c\), which by step 10 lies in both intervals. So the difference of the two mixed derivatives at \(P\) is the sum of the differences of step 10:
    \[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\,\partial y}(P) - \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\,\partial x}(P) &= \Big(\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\,\partial y}(P) - \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\,\partial y}(Q_1)\Big) \\ &\quad + \Big(\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\,\partial x}(Q_2) - \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\,\partial x}(P)\Big) . \end{aligned}\]
    By the triangle inequality for numbers, \(|a + b| \le |a| + |b|\) (lemma 1.6, item 1), and by step 10 the absolute value of the left-hand side is less than \(\eta/2 + \eta/2 = \eta\).
  12. We picked the error \(\eta\) freely. The absolute value of the difference of the two mixed derivatives at \(P\) is not negative and is smaller than every positive number, so by lemma 1.34 on an inequality tested with all positive numbers it equals zero. The mixed derivatives at \(P\) are equal.
  13. For the variables \(x\) and \(z\) and for \(y\) and \(z\) steps 1 to 12 are the same, only with the variables renamed.

Source: LEBL2 Prop. 8.6.2 (PDF pp. 60-62). The source assumes that all partial derivatives up to second order are continuous at all points of an open set, and remarks that continuity of the two mixed derivatives is enough. The proof uses continuity only at the point \(P\). Steps 9 to 12 replace the limit of a function of two variables used by the source and are not from the source.

The proof wrote the double difference twice as the product of \(s\,t\) and a mixed derivative, once with one order of differentiation and once with the other, each time at some point inside the rectangle. As the rectangle shrinks, both points approach \(P\), and the continuity of the mixed derivatives makes their values approach the values at \(P\). The mean value theorem did the same job here, twice, as for the change of a field over a short step in section 1.15: it turned a difference of values into a derivative at a point in between.

Is the assumption of continuity needed? It is. In Exercise 8.6.2 (PDF p. 62), LEBL2 gives the function of two variables

\[f(x, y) = \frac{x\,y\,(x^2 - y^2)}{x^2 + y^2} \quad \text{for } (x, y) \neq (0, 0) , \qquad f(0, 0) = 0 ,\]

whose first order partial derivatives exist and are continuous, while the mixed derivatives exist but are not continuous at the origin and differ there. On the axis \(y\) the difference quotient with respect to \(x\) is \(\big(f(h, y) - f(0, y)\big)/h = y\,(h^2 - y^2)/(h^2 + y^2)\), and as \(h\) goes to zero with \(y \neq 0\), the numerator approaches \(-y^3\), the denominator \(y^2\), and the quotient \(-y\). So \(\partial f / \partial x\,(0, y) = -y\), and this holds at \(y = 0\) too, since \(f\) is zero everywhere on the axis \(x\). In the same way we get the value \(\partial f / \partial y\,(x, 0) = x\) on the axis \(x\). Therefore \(\partial^2 f / \partial y\,\partial x\,(0, 0) = -1\), \(\partial^2 f / \partial x\,\partial y\,(0, 0) = 1\) (figure 1.389). That the two are not both continuous at the origin is already told by the theorem: if both were continuous, they would be equal by the theorem, but they are \(-1\) and \(1\). The source adds that neither of them is continuous at the origin. For the hanging bar and for the strips of this section the displacement components are polynomials. Their partial derivatives of all orders are polynomials again, and these are continuous everywhere by corollary 1.69, that polynomials in \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\) are continuous.

Let us draw these two first derivatives. On the left graph the blue line is the derivative \(\partial f / \partial x\,(0, y)\) as a function of \(y\), which equals \(-y\). The slope of the line is \(-1\): for a step \(h\) to the right the value changes by \(-h\). This is the mixed derivative \(\partial^2 f / \partial y\,\partial x\,(0, 0) = -1\). On the right graph the blue line is the derivative \(\partial f / \partial y\,(x, 0)\) as a function of \(x\), which equals \(x\). Its slope is \(1\), and this is the mixed derivative \(\partial^2 f / \partial x\,\partial y\,(0, 0) = 1\). The lines slope in opposite directions, so the mixed derivatives at the origin are not equal.

In the equations we are looking for we will differentiate three times and swap the order in several places. So we extend the theorem to third derivatives. We draw the six orders \(a\,b\,c\) as a hexagon (figure 1.390). Each corner is one order of differentiation, we start at \(a\,b\,c\) at the top. Each side is one swap of two neighbouring letters. The blue sides swap the first two letters, the outer pair, the blackwhite ones swap the last two, the inner pair. Blue and blackwhite alternate, because the same swap twice in a row would bring back the previous order. By alternating we go around all six orders and after six swaps we come to \(a\,b\,c\) again.

Corollary 1.126 Independence of the order of differentiation (neodvisnost od vrstnega reda odvajanja)

Let \(D\) be a set of points in which every point is interior, that is, around every point \(P\) of \(D\) there is a number \(r > 0\) such that all points whose distance from \(P\) is less than \(r\) are in \(D\). Let a function \(f\) have partial derivatives of first, second and third order at every point of \(D\), and let all these derivatives be continuous at every point of \(D\). Then at every point of \(D\) the second and third partial derivatives of \(f\) do not depend on the order in which we differentiate.

Proof

We must show that for second and third partial derivatives a swap of the order of differentiation does not change the value. Let \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\) be variables, each of them \(x\), \(y\) or \(z\).

1. Second derivatives.

  1. Let \(P\) be a point of \(D\) and \(r\) its number from the assumption. The function \(f\) is defined at all points whose distance from \(P\) is less than \(r\), its first and second partial derivatives exist there, and the mixed derivatives are continuous at \(P\). By theorem 1.125 on the symmetry of mixed partial derivatives (figure 1.388, the values \(m_1\) and \(m_2\) are equal), \(\partial^2 f / \partial a\,\partial b\,(P) = \partial^2 f / \partial b\,\partial a\,(P)\).

2. Third derivatives.

  1. Swapping the inner pair. By the first part, the functions \(\partial^2 f / \partial b\,\partial c\) and \(\partial^2 f / \partial c\,\partial b\) are equal at every point of \(D\). Equal functions have equal difference quotients and so equal partial derivatives, therefore \(\partial^3 f / \partial a\,\partial b\,\partial c = \partial^3 f / \partial a\,\partial c\,\partial b\) at every point of \(D\).
  2. Swapping the outer pair. Let \(h = \partial f / \partial c\). Its first partial derivatives are second partial derivatives of \(f\), and its second partial derivatives are third partial derivatives of \(f\), which exist and are continuous. By theorem 1.125 applied to \(h\), \(\partial^2 h / \partial a\,\partial b = \partial^2 h / \partial b\,\partial a\), that is, \(\partial^3 f / \partial a\,\partial b\,\partial c = \partial^3 f / \partial b\,\partial a\,\partial c\) at every point of \(D\).
  3. From the order \(a\,b\,c\) we get all six orders by a chain of swaps, each time swapping either the outer or the inner pair:
    \[a\,b\,c \to b\,a\,c \to b\,c\,a \to c\,b\,a \to c\,a\,b \to a\,c\,b .\]
    By steps 1 and 2 no swap changes the value, so all orders are equivalent. If two of the variables are equal, there are fewer different orders, but the chain still covers them all.

Source: LEBL2 Exercise 8.6.3 (PDF p. 62) states the claim for derivatives of any order. The proof is not from the source.

A function whose partial derivatives up to third order exist and are continuous at every point of a set is called by LEBL2 a three times continuously differentiable function (LEBL2 Def. 8.6.1, PDF p. 60). For a displacement field this is more than the continuous differentiability of definition 1.90 requires. The body has no cracks, and the strains and their first and second partial derivatives change from point to point without jumps. We will need this assumption for the equations we are looking for. It fails, for example, at a crack or at a point where a force concentrated at one point acts on the body (section 1.15).

1.18.3 Compatibility equations

Let us return to the strip of section 1.18.1. A thin steel strip of length 200 mm and height 20 mm lies in the plane of the axes \(x\) and \(y\), the axis \(x\) along the strip, the origin at the middle of the left end. We prescribed the strains (1.64) to it, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = k\,y^2\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\), with \(k = -10\) m⁻². Let us show that there is no displacement field with these strains. Let us first draw the idea (figure 1.391). On the left, the grey dashed lines are two longitudinal fibres before the deformation, the lower at the height \(y = 0\) and the upper at \(y = 5\) mm, straight, because the strip is still straight. The arrows between the halves show the directions of the axes \(x\) and \(y\), which hold for both halves: the fibres lie in the direction of the axis \(x\), the displacement \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) is vertical. The orange curves are the fibres after the deformation. Everything is greatly magnified. The curves are equal, only shifted. This is what \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0\) demands: the transverse fibres keep their length, so the points of both fibres at the same \(x\) move equally in the direction of the axis \(y\) (step 1 below). The blue dimensions stand on the same vertical line, that is, at the same value of \(x\), and show the displacement \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) of each fibre. They are equally long. On the right the dashed lines are again the fibres before the deformation. The lower orange line is the fibre at \(y = 0\), as the strains demand it: straight, so the label beside it has the second derivative zero. The upper orange curve is the fibre at \(y = 5\) mm, curved, with the second derivative \(0{,}1\ \text{m}^{-1}\). Both start with the same slope, so that the difference is only in the curvature. The two pictures contradict each other: the left demands the same shape for both fibres, the right two different curvatures. So there is no displacement field. Let us also write the idea in two lines:

  • the transverse fibres keep their length (\(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0\)), so both fibres bend into the same shape \(u_{\mathrm{y}}(x)\) (steps 1 and 2 below),
  • without shear (\(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\)), however, the fibre at the height \(y\) must curve so that \(\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x^2 = -\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} / \partial y = -2k\,y\), that is \(0\) at \(y = 0\) and \(0{,}1\ \text{m}^{-1}\) at \(y = 5\) mm (steps 3 to 6).

The same shape cannot have two different second derivatives. The bands at these heights therefore curve differently, as in figure 1.383, right. We argue by contradiction: suppose that at the interior points of the strip there is a displacement field whose components have continuous partial derivatives of first and second order and which gives these strains.

  1. Since \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial y = 0\) at every point, \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) has derivative zero along every transverse segment on which \(x\) and \(z\) are constant. By corollary 1.85 on a function with zero derivative, applied on the interval between \(0\) and \(y\), we have \(u_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y, z) = u_{\mathrm{y}}(x, 0, z)\) for every \(y\). All points of a transverse segment move equally in the direction of the axis \(y\).
  2. So \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x\) and \(\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x^2\) do not depend on \(y\) either, both fibres have the same shape. Indeed, at the points \((x, y, z)\) and \((x, 0, z)\) the difference quotients with respect to \(x\) are equal, because the values are equal, and so their limits are equal too.
  3. Since \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\), by (1.63) \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial y + \partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x = 0\), that is, \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x = -\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial y\) at every point. The right angle between a longitudinal and a transverse fibre stays right, so the longitudinal fibre turns by the same angle by which the transverse fibre tilts.
  4. Equal functions have equal partial derivatives with respect to \(x\): \(\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x^2 = -\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial x\,\partial y\).
  5. By theorem 1.125 on the symmetry of mixed partial derivatives, \(\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial x\,\partial y = \partial^2 u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial y\,\partial x = \partial / \partial y\,(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial x) = \partial \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} / \partial y\).
  6. For the prescribed strain \(\partial \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} / \partial y = \partial(k\,y^2)/\partial y = 2k\,y\) (lemma 1.81 on the rules of differentiation). With steps 4 and 5, the second derivative of the fibre at the height \(y\) is
    \[\frac{\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x^2} = -2k\,y .\]
  7. By step 2 the left-hand side does not depend on \(y\), but the right-hand side does. At \(y = 0\) the right-hand side is \(0\), at \(y = 5\) mm it is \(-2 \cdot (-10\ \text{m}^{-2}) \cdot 0{,}005\ \text{m} = 0{,}1\ \text{m}^{-1}\). This is a contradiction, so there is no displacement field with the prescribed strains.

The computation also tells us why the bands in figure 1.383 curve. The partial derivative \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x\) is the slope of a longitudinal fibre after straining: how much the fibre rises per unit length. The second derivative \(\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x^2\) says how fast this slope changes along the fibre. A fibre that has the same slope everywhere is straight. The faster the slope changes, the more strongly the fibre is curved. Steps 3 to 6 say that in a strip without shear \(\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x^2 = -\partial \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} / \partial y\): the longitudinal fibre at the height \(y\) curves the more strongly, the faster the strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) changes with height there. Steps 1 and 2 say that when the transverse fibres keep their length, all longitudinal fibres curve equally. Both requirements can hold together only if \(\partial \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} / \partial y\) is the same at all heights. For \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = y/R\) we have \(\partial \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} / \partial y = 1/R\) everywhere, and indeed \(\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x^2 = \partial^2(-x^2/(2R))/\partial x^2 = -1/R\). For \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = k\,y^2\), though, \(2k\,y\) differs at different heights.

Why a fibre curves when the strain changes with height is shown in figure 1.392. Let us draw a piece of the strip. The blackwhite rectangle is the piece before the deformation, \(\Delta x\) wide and \(\Delta y\) high. Its bottom and top sides are short longitudinal fibres of length \(\Delta x\) at the heights \(y\) and \(y + \Delta y\), which start on the same transverse fibre, the left edge. In orange is the piece after the deformation, if the longitudinal fibres stayed horizontal. The left edge stays in place, because we do not move it. The right ends of the fibres move to the right by different lengths, and four grey dashed lines carry the original and new ends of both fibres to the grey dimensions above the piece and below it. The deformation is greatly magnified so that it can be seen. The upper one lengthens by \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}(y + \Delta y)\,\Delta x\), the lower one by \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}(y)\,\Delta x\). If the two strains differ, the right ends move by different amounts, and the transverse fibre on the right tilts relative to the one on the left. Its upper end moves horizontally farther than the lower one by the difference of the two lengthenings, at the height \(\Delta y\). The fibre therefore tilts by

\[\frac{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}(y + \Delta y)\,\Delta x - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}(y)\,\Delta x}{\Delta y} = \frac{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}(y + \Delta y) - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}(y)}{\Delta y}\,\Delta x\]

horizontal distances per unit height. Since the right angles are to stay right, the longitudinal fibres turn together with the tilted transverse fibre, and their slope changes over the length \(\Delta x\) by about as much, downward if the upper fibre lengthens more. Per unit length, the slope of the longitudinal fibre therefore changes by about \(-\big(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}(y + \Delta y) - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}(y)\big)/\Delta y\), and as \(\Delta y\) gets shorter this quotient approaches \(\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} / \partial y\). So the figure shows where the equality \(\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x^2 = -\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} / \partial y\) from steps 3 to 6 comes from. The next piece in the row turns a little more, and so the row of pieces curves. In the right figure the blackwhite pieces are four pieces in a row before the deformation. The orange curves are their longitudinal fibres after the deformation, the lower one lengthens less, the upper one more, and so they are two arcs around the same centre. The orange transverse lines are the transverse fibres: they stay perpendicular to the fibres, so they are tilted more and more.

What if the transverse fibres do not keep their length, or the right angles change? Let us draw this strip. The grey dashed rectangle with five horizontal lines is the strip before the deformation, with five longitudinal fibres at different heights. The orange curves are these fibres after the deformation, greatly magnified. The middle fibre stays straight, the others curve, the more the farther from the middle they are, and each differently. The thick orange curve on the right is the right transverse fibre after the deformation. It is longer than the original, because the longitudinal fibres have spread apart. Then the longitudinal fibres at different heights can curve differently. If, for example, the transverse fibres lengthen by \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = -k\,x^2\), that is, more and more toward the right end of the strip, the strains

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = k\,y^2 , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = -k\,x^2 , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\]

come from the field \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = k\,x\,y^2\), \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = -k\,x^2\,y\), \(u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\). Indeed \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial x = k\,y^2\), \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial y = -k\,x^2\) and \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial y + \partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x = 2k\,x\,y - 2k\,x\,y = 0\). Since the transverse fibres lengthen, step 1 of the proof above no longer holds. The longitudinal fibre at the height \(y\) now has the shape \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = -k\,x^2\,y\), which depends on \(y\), with the second derivative \(\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x^2 = -2k\,y\). This is exactly the second derivative that step 6 requires, so the fibres at different heights can curve differently.

With \(k = -10\) m⁻², however, this example is no longer one of small strains. At the right end of the strip, at \(x = 200\) mm, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = 10\ \text{m}^{-2} \cdot (0{,}2\ \text{m})^2 = 0{,}4\), \(400\) times the bound \(0{,}001\) that the small deformation assumption sets for steel structures (section 1.17.3), and there the small strain tensor no longer tells accurately how much the fibres lengthen. The number \(k\) is therefore strongly exaggerated. We kept it only so that the strip can be compared with the first strip. The condition that we will test on the strips is an exact relation between second partial derivatives of the components \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), which the components computed from a displacement field satisfy, whatever the size of \(k\). The size of \(k\) decides only whether these components still describe the lengthening of the fibres accurately. All computations of this section are linear in \(k\): at another \(k\) the strains, the displacements and all their derivatives are only multiplied by the same number. With \(k = -0{,}025\) m⁻² the largest strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) would be exactly \(0{,}001\), while \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) at the edges would be only \(2{,}5 \cdot 10^{-6}\), and everything that follows would hold in the same way. The general condition, which says how much the strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and the shear \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) must make up for fibres at different heights curving differently, is the first of the six equations in the following theorem.

From history

Let us draw a timeline. The axis shows years. The relations given by the theorem below were first obtained by Saint-Venant in 1864, without using rotations. The proof that he indicated was developed later by Gustav Robert Kirchhoff, and the proof through rotations is the work of Eugenio Beltrami, published in 1889 (LOVE, PDF pp. 68-69).

The six equations that the components of the strain, calculated from the displacement field, satisfy are given by the following theorem. Before we read them, let us draw their pattern (figure 1.395). The three corners of the triangle are the axes \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\). The blue arrows beside the sides show the renaming of the axes \(x \to y \to z \to x\) and close into a circle. The numbers are the equations that we will list. In the renaming each side goes to the next one, so equation 1 goes to equation 2, and this at the next renaming to equation 3. Each corner goes to the next one, so equation 4 goes to equation 5, and this to equation 6. The proof therefore derives only equations 1 and 4, and gets the other four by renaming. Let us write down their pattern:

  • equations 1 to 3, which are beside the sides in the figure, one for each of the planes \(x\)-\(y\), \(y\)-\(z\) and \(z\)-\(x\): second derivatives of both normal strains in the directions of this plane and of the shear in it,
  • equations 4 to 6, which are beside the corners in the figure, one for each of the axes \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\): second derivatives of the normal strain in the direction of this axis and of the shears in all three planes.
Theorem 1.127 Compatibility equations (enačbe kompatibilnosti)

Let \(D\) be a set of points in which every point is interior, and let the components \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) of a displacement field have, at every point of \(D\), partial derivatives of first, second and third order that are continuous at every point of \(D\). Then the strain components (1.63) satisfy, at every point of \(D\), the equations

\[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial y^2} + \frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}}{\partial x^2} &= 2\,\frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial x\,\partial y} , \\ \frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}}{\partial z^2} + \frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}}{\partial y^2} &= 2\,\frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}}{\partial y\,\partial z} , \\ \frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial z^2} &= 2\,\frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}}{\partial x\,\partial z} , \\ \frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial y\,\partial z} + \frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}}{\partial x^2} &= \frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}}{\partial x\,\partial y} + \frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial x\,\partial z} , \\ \frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}}{\partial x\,\partial z} + \frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}}{\partial y^2} &= \frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial y\,\partial z} + \frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}}{\partial x\,\partial y} , \\ \frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}}{\partial x\,\partial y} + \frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial z^2} &= \frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}}{\partial x\,\partial z} + \frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}}{\partial y\,\partial z} . \end{aligned} \tag{1.68}\]
Proof

We must show that each of the six equations holds when we put the components (1.63) into it. The strain components are first partial derivatives of the displacements or halves of their sums, so their second partial derivatives are third partial derivatives of the displacements. By corollary 1.126 on the independence of the order of differentiation, the third partial derivatives of the displacements do not depend on the order of differentiation. We compute partial derivatives as ordinary derivatives, so the two rules of lemma 1.81 hold for them: the derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives, and a constant factor can be taken out.

1. The first equation.

  1. Since \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial x\), \(\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} / \partial y^2\) is a third partial derivative of \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\), once with respect to \(x\) and twice with respect to \(y\). By the same corollary we can write it as
    \[\frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial y^2} = \frac{\partial^2}{\partial x\,\partial y}\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y}\Big) .\]
  2. Since \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial y\), \(\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} / \partial x^2\) is a third partial derivative of \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\), once with respect to \(y\) and twice with respect to \(x\). By the same corollary,
    \[\frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}}{\partial x^2} = \frac{\partial^2}{\partial x\,\partial y}\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x}\Big) .\]
  3. We add the equalities of steps 1 and 2. The derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives, so
    \[\frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial y^2} + \frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}}{\partial x^2} = \frac{\partial^2}{\partial x\,\partial y}\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x}\Big) .\]
  4. By (1.63) the sum in the bracket is \(2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\). We take out the constant factor \(2\) and get the first equation of (1.68).

2. The second and third equations.

  1. We rename the axes: \(x\) to \(y\), \(y\) to \(z\) and \(z\) to \(x\). The components of the strain are renamed as follows:
    \[\begin{aligned} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} &\to \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} , & \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} &\to \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} , & \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} &\to \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} , \\ \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} &\to \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} , & \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} &\to \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} , & \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} &\to \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} . \end{aligned}\]
    The equations (1.63) then turn into each other. From \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial x\) we get \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial y\), from \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) we get \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\), and from \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) we get \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}}\), which by definition equals \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\). The assumption of the theorem does not change either. So the steps of the first part hold with the renamed axes, and the first equation becomes
    \[\frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}}{\partial z^2} + \frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}}{\partial y^2} = 2\,\frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}}{\partial y\,\partial z} ,\]
    which is the second equation.
  2. When we rename the axes once more in the same way, the second equation becomes the third. In it \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) appears, and by corollary 1.126 on the independence of the order of differentiation the order of differentiation in \(\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} / \partial z\,\partial x\) does not matter.

3. The fourth equation. What part of each of the three third derivatives each term contains is drawn in figure 1.396. The figure has three pairs of columns, one for each third derivative of the displacements, which the label above the pair writes: the first pair for the derivative of \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) with respect to \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\), the second for the derivative of \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) twice with respect to \(x\) and once with respect to \(z\) and the third for the derivative of \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) twice with respect to \(x\) and once with respect to \(y\). In each pair the left column is the sum of the terms of the left side of the equation, the right one the sum of the terms of the right side, and between them is the sign \(=\). The height of a column is the share of this third derivative that the term contains. A whole derivative is 1 high. For each of the three derivatives the two columns are equally high, which means that the share of this derivative is the same on both sides. Each term has its own colour, which the legend under the columns tells: the first term of the left side in blue, the second term of the left side in grey, the first term of the right side in orange and the second term of the right side in blackwhite. Each section of a column in the colour of a term is the share contributed by that term. We write the terms in order.

  1. We write each term with the displacements by (1.63). The first term on the left is a third partial derivative of \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\), with respect to \(x\), to \(y\) and to \(z\):
    \[\frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial y\,\partial z} = \frac{\partial^2}{\partial y\,\partial z}\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x}\Big) .\]
  2. The second term on the left is
    \[\frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}}{\partial x^2} = \frac12\,\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2}\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial z}\Big) + \frac12\,\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2}\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial y}\Big) ,\]
    the third partial derivative of \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) twice with respect to \(x\) and once with respect to \(z\), and the third partial derivative of \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) twice with respect to \(x\) and once with respect to \(y\), each with the factor \(\tfrac12\).
  3. The first term on the right is
    \[\frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}}{\partial x\,\partial y} = \frac12\,\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x\,\partial y}\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial z}\Big) + \frac12\,\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x\,\partial y}\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial x}\Big) ,\]
    half of the third partial derivative of \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) with respect to \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\), and half of the third partial derivative of \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) twice with respect to \(x\) and once with respect to \(y\).
  4. The second term on the right is
    \[\frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial x\,\partial z} = \frac12\,\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x\,\partial z}\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y}\Big) + \frac12\,\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x\,\partial z}\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x}\Big) ,\]
    half of the third partial derivative of \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) with respect to \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\), and half of the third partial derivative of \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) twice with respect to \(x\) and once with respect to \(z\).
  5. By corollary 1.126 on the independence of the order of differentiation, third derivatives of the same component with respect to the same variables are equal, whatever the order. On the right-hand side the two halves of the derivative of \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) with respect to \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\) therefore add up to the whole derivative, which equals the first term on the left from step 1. The half of the derivative of \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) from step 3 equals the second half from step 2, and the half of the derivative of \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) from step 4 equals the first half from step 2. So the right-hand side equals the left-hand side, and the fourth equation holds.

Overview of steps 1 to 5: what part of each of the three third derivatives each term contains:

term \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) with respect to \(x\), \(y\), \(z\) \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) twice with respect to \(x\), once to \(z\) \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) twice with respect to \(x\), once to \(y\)
left: \(\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} / \partial y\,\partial z\) \(1\) \(0\) \(0\)
left: \(\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} / \partial x^2\) \(0\) \(\tfrac12\) \(\tfrac12\)
right: \(\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} / \partial x\,\partial y\) \(\tfrac12\) \(0\) \(\tfrac12\)
right: \(\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} / \partial x\,\partial z\) \(\tfrac12\) \(\tfrac12\) \(0\)

The sum of the first two rows is \(1\), \(\tfrac12\), \(\tfrac12\), and the sum of the last two is equal to it (the columns in each pair are equally tall).

4. The fifth and sixth equations.

  1. When we rename the axes in the fourth equation as in the second part, \(x\) to \(y\), \(y\) to \(z\) and \(z\) to \(x\), and use \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\) and the fact that the order of differentiation does not matter, we get the fifth equation. One more renaming gives the sixth.

Source: CM (3.7.4)-(3.7.9) (PDF pp. 150-151), SADD (2.6.2) (PDF p. 51), BARBER (2.8)-(2.9) (PDF p. 45). CM derives the first equation and only states the others, SADD derives them in index notation.

The equations (1.68) are called the Saint-Venant compatibility equations (CM, PDF p. 149, SADD, PDF p. 51). The proof showed where they come from: the strain components are derivatives of only three functions, and when we differentiate them twice more, the same third derivatives of the displacements appear in several places. The equations are exactly these repetitions, written without the displacements.

Let us test the equations on three strips. For the strip with the strains (1.64), \(\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} / \partial y^2 = \partial(2k\,y)/\partial y = 2k\), while the other two terms of the first equation are zero, because \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) are zero. The first equation would require \(2k + 0 = 0\), but for \(k = -10\) m⁻² the left-hand side is \(-20\) m⁻². The equation fails, so by the theorem no displacement field with continuous derivatives up to third order gives these strains, as we already showed above. For the strip with \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = y/R\), on the other hand, \(\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} / \partial y^2 = 0\), and the first equation holds, \(0 + 0 = 0\). For the corrected strip with \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = -k\,x^2\) we have \(\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} / \partial x^2 = -2k\), and the first equation holds, \(2k - 2k = 0\). The other five equations hold for all three strips, because no component depends on \(z\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\) are zero. All three strips at a glance:

strip \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) left side of the first equation right side displacement field
first \(k\,y^2\) \(0\) \(0\) \(2k\) \(0\) none
second \(y/R\) \(0\) \(0\) \(0\) \(0\) \((x\,y/R,\ -x^2/(2R),\ 0)\)
third \(k\,y^2\) \(-k\,x^2\) \(0\) \(2k - 2k = 0\) \(0\) \((k\,x\,y^2,\ -k\,x^2\,y,\ 0)\)

What does the first equation say in words? By the computation on the strip and by figure 1.392, where the transverse fibre tilts, \(-\partial \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} / \partial y\) is how strongly a longitudinal fibre curves when there is no shear. So the term \(\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} / \partial y^2\) says how fast this curving changes with height. The term \(\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} / \partial x^2\) says the same for the transverse fibres, with the roles of the axes swapped. The shear term on the right says how much the change of right angles lets the fibres curve differently than the left side requires. The left-hand side must equal the right-hand side, otherwise the pieces do not fit together.

An example: the strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = k\,y^2\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = k\,x\,y\) come from the field \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = k\,x\,y^2\), \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = 0\), \(u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\), since \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial x = k\,y^2\) and \(\tfrac12\,(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial y + \partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x) = \tfrac12 \cdot 2k\,x\,y\). Let us draw the strip. The grey dashed grid is the strip before the deformation, with five longitudinal and five transverse fibres. The fifth transverse fibre is the left edge, \(x = 0\), which stays in place, because \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\) there. The deformation is greatly magnified. In orange are the fibres after the deformation. The longitudinal fibres do not curve at all here, because \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = 0\). Instead four transverse fibres curve. Each is a parabola, because a point at the height \(y\) moves horizontally by \(k\,x\,y^2\), the more the farther from the middle it is. So the right angles change. At \(x = 3\) and \(y = \pm 1\) the grey tangents of the transverse fibre are drawn, both directed upward, in the direction of increasing \(y\). The grey arcs measure the angle from the direction of the axis \(x\) to these tangents. At the top the tangent points out of the strip, so the arc is above the strip, at the bottom it points into the strip. Before the deformation this angle is a right angle, after it it is \(125{,}8^\circ\) at the top and \(54{,}2^\circ\) at the bottom. The first equation holds: the left side is \(2k + 0\), the right side \(2\,\partial^2(k\,x\,y)/\partial x\,\partial y = 2k\). The factor \(2\) is on the right because \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) is only half of the sum \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial y + \partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x\). The left side must equal the right side, otherwise the pieces do not fit together.

For the hanging bar the test is short. A steel bar of length \(L = 10\) m hangs under its own weight, the axis \(x\) pointing down from the centre \(O\) of the top end. By (1.63) and the table of partial derivatives in section 1.7.2 its strains are

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = 2a\,(L - x) , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x) , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0 .\]

Let us draw the strains over the depth. The axes are the depth \(x\) and the strain. The blue line is \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = 2a\,(L - x)\), which falls from the value \(2aL\) at the top to zero at \(x = L\). Below the cross-section at \(x = L\) nothing hangs that would pull it, since the pull in the bar falls from the weight of the whole bar at the top to zero at the lower end (section 1.2). Without a pull the material does not stretch there. The blackwhite line is \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\), with the value \(-0{,}6\,aL\) at the top. It lies below the axis, because the bar is contracted in the transverse direction, and it rises to zero at \(x = L\). The slope of a line is its derivative. For both it is constant, \(-2a\) for the blue one and \(0{,}6\,a\) for the blackwhite one.

The shear strains are zero because the pairs of partial derivatives off the diagonal of the table cancel, for example \(\tfrac12\,(-0{,}6\,a\,y + 0{,}6\,a\,y) = 0\). In the first equation \(\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} / \partial y^2\) and \(\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} / \partial x^2\) are zero. The first is zero because \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) does not depend on \(y\). The second is zero because \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) is a straight line in \(x\) with the derivative \(0{,}6\,a\), which is constant and has derivative zero. The right-hand side is zero because \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) is zero. The equation holds, \(0 + 0 = 0\). In the same way, in all the other equations all second derivatives of the strains are zero, because the strains depend only on \(x\), and at most linearly. It must be so, since we got the strains from a displacement field whose components are polynomials and so have continuous derivatives of all orders.

A few remarks on the equations.

  1. In plane problems, where \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) depend only on \(x\) and \(y\) and \(u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\), the strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\) are zero and no strain depends on \(z\). Only the first equation remains, and the other five turn into \(0 = 0\) (BARBER, PDF p. 45).
  2. Books that use the engineering shear strain \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) write the first equation as \(\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} / \partial y^2 + \partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} / \partial x^2 = \partial^2 \gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} / \partial x\,\partial y\), without the factor \(2\). CM writes the components \(\varepsilon_{11}\), \(\varepsilon_{12}\) and the coordinates \(X_1\), \(X_2\), SADD writes \(e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(e_{\mathrm{xy}}\), both with half the shear as we do.
