  3. We might expect three equations, since six functions come from three, \(6 - 3 = 3\). In the plane counting works: the three functions \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) come from two, \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\), and one equation remains, the first (remark 1). In space, though, there are six equations, and none of them can be derived from the other five (BARBER, PDF p. 45). We see the reason in (1.68): every equation contains second derivatives that appear in no other one, the first for example \(\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} / \partial y^2\). For each equation we can therefore find strains that satisfy the other five but not it. For the first these are the strains of the first strip, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = k\,y^2\), with the others zero. So none of the six equations may be left out. SADD (PDF p. 51), however, says that the six equations are not independent, because there are relations among them involving derivatives, and that they can be reduced to three independent equations of fourth order. This does not contradict BARBER, since the relations are among the derivatives of the equations, not among the equations themselves. We denote by \(R_1, \dots, R_6\) the left side of each of the six equations minus its right side. For any six functions with continuous partial derivatives up to the third order,
    \[\frac{\partial R_2}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial R_6}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial R_5}{\partial z} .\]
    This follows when we insert \(R_2\), \(R_5\) and \(R_6\) and interchange the order of differentiation by corollary 1.126 (we checked the computation with SymPy). Two similar relations follow by renaming the axes. If the fifth and sixth equations hold, the relation gives only \(\partial R_2 / \partial x = 0\): \(R_2\) does not change in the direction of the axis \(x\), but it need not be zero. The second equation does not follow from the fifth and sixth, but its derivative with respect to \(x\) does. Conclusions from counting equations with numbers for equations with derivatives therefore do not always hold (BARBER, PDF p. 45). We get three equations, as the counting suggests, only with fourth derivatives.
  4. The equations hold for the small strain tensor. For the Green-Lagrange strain tensor (definition 1.112) there are conditions for fitting together too. CM writes them with the deformation gradient, while the form with the Green-Lagrange tensor is so involved that it does not derive it (CM, PDF pp. 149 and 154).
  5. We need the equations only when we solve a problem with strains or with forces in the material, not with displacements. When we first find the displacements and compute the strains from them, the strains fit together by themselves (CM, PDF p. 154, SADD, PDF p. 54). We will use them in chapter 11.

1.18.4 A field without strain

Theorem 1.127 gave a condition that the strains satisfy when they come from a displacement field. Before we ask whether the condition is also enough, let us answer another question. Suppose that a displacement field with the given strains exists. Is it the only one? For the bar we got the answer in section 1.14.6: two displacements of the bar that have the same strain at every point differ only by the same shift of all points (corollary 1.85 on a function with zero derivative). In space we expect more freedom. We can shift a body as a whole and also turn it, like the square plate in figure 1.409, without changing the distance between any two of its points (section 1.6). Such a rigid-body displacement changes the length of no fibre, so we can add it to every displacement field.

For a true rotation that keeps all distances, though, the small strain tensor shows a strain that is not there, even when the rotation is small. In section 1.17.6 we turned a square plate about the axis \(z\) with the numbers \(s = 0{,}001\) and \(c = \sqrt{1 - s^2}\) and got \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = c - 1 = -5{,}0 \cdot 10^{-7}\), although the plate was not strained. Which displacements have a small strain tensor of exactly zero? In section 1.17.5 we stated that a displacement given by an antisymmetric matrix that is the same at all points is a rigid rotation when the entries of the matrix are small (CM, PDF p. 143). Let us add to it a shift of all points by the same vector. We get the field

\[\vek u(P) = \vek a + \mat W\,\vek r_{\mathrm{P}} ,\]

where \(\vek a\) is a constant vector, \(\mat W\) a constant antisymmetric matrix (definition 1.102), and \(\vek r_{\mathrm{P}} = \overrightarrow{OP} = (x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}}, z_{\mathrm{P}})\) the vector from the origin \(O\) to the point \(P\), whose components are the coordinates of \(P\). The component \(\ix{i}\) of the displacement is \(u_{\mathrm{i}}(P) = a_{\mathrm{i}} + \sum_{\mathrm{j}} W_{\mathrm{ij}}\,x_{\mathrm{j}}(P)\), where as before \(x_{\mathrm{x}} = x\), \(x_{\mathrm{y}} = y\) and \(x_{\mathrm{z}} = z\). The partial derivative of this component with respect to \(x_{\mathrm{j}}\) is \(W_{\mathrm{ij}}\): the number \(a_{\mathrm{i}}\) is constant, the coordinate \(x_{\mathrm{j}}\) has the derivative \(1\) with respect to itself, and the other two coordinates are constant in this differentiation (lemma 1.81 on the rules of differentiation). So the displacement gradient is \(\mat W\) at every point, and the small strain tensor is \(\tfrac12(\mat W + \mat W^\T) = \tfrac12(\mat W - \mat W) = \mat 0\). The small rotation tensor is \(\tfrac12(\mat W - \mat W^\T) = \mat W\). An example is a rotation about the axis \(z\), for which the matrix has a single pair of nonzero entries:

\[\mat W = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -s & 0 \\ s & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} , \qquad \mat W\,\vek r_{\mathrm{P}} = (-s\,y_{\mathrm{P}},\ s\,x_{\mathrm{P}},\ 0) .\]

Let us draw this, seen from above, along the axis \(z\). On the left the blackwhite square is the plate before the movement, with the corner \(O\) at the origin. Its opposite corner is the point \(P\). The grey dashed line from \(O\) to \(P\) is the vector \(\vek r_{\mathrm{P}}\). The rotation is greatly magnified: instead of \(s = 0{,}001\), \(s = 0{,}3\) is drawn, so that it can be seen. The point \(P\) moves perpendicular to the vector \((x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}}, 0)\) that points from the axis \(z\) to it, by \(s\) times its length. The blue arrow is this displacement \(\mat W\,\vek r_{\mathrm{P}}\), the grey right-angle mark shows that it is perpendicular to the line \(O P\). All four corners move by the same rule, perpendicular to their line from \(O\). The orange square is therefore the plate turned about \(O\). For such a large \(s\) it is also slightly larger than the blackwhite one. The displacement of the point \(P\) is perpendicular to \(\vek r_{\mathrm{P}}\) and \(s\,|\vek r_{\mathrm{P}}|\) long, so by the Pythagorean theorem the new distance of \(P\) from \(O\) is \(\sqrt{1 + s^2}\,|\vek r_{\mathrm{P}}|\). The same computation holds for every side, since the difference of the displacements of its end points is \(\mat W\) times the vector of the side. The sides therefore lengthen \(\sqrt{1 + s^2}\) times, at \(s = 0{,}3\) by \(4{,}4\) %, and at \(s = 0{,}001\) by only \(5 \cdot 10^{-7}\) of their length. On the right is the same square with the corner \(O\), the point \(P\), the line \(O P\) and the blue arrow, which as on the left shows the displacement of \(P\) in the rotation. To all points we add also the constant shift \(\vek a\), drawn at \(O\) and at the turned point \(P\), at the end of the blue arrow. The displacement is the same vector everywhere, so the turned square moves as a whole and does not deform. The orange square on the right is the plate after the rotation and the shift. We will test such a field on the square plate of figure 1.409.

The goal of this section is to show the converse: a displacement field whose small strain tensor is zero at every point of a body has the form \(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r\). From this the answer to the question at the start will follow. Two displacement fields that have the same strains at every point differ only by \(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r\), that is, by a shift of all points and a small rotation of the body as a whole. There are three assumptions. The displacement field is continuously differentiable (definition 1.90), as we have assumed all along since section 1.15.6. We look at it at the interior points of the body, which form an open set (lemma 1.89 on the neighbourhood of an interior point). The body is in one piece. We will state the last assumption precisely, because without it the claim fails. The route is this. First we look at what the strains say about the rotation, when the field has continuous second partial derivatives. We test this lemma on the hanging bar and will need it in the next section, while the theorem we prove without it, with first derivatives only. For the theorem we say when a set of points is in one piece, and show that a ring is. We also prepare three tools: the distance to the points of a segment, the derivative along a segment, and the constancy of a function with zero partial derivatives on a set in one piece. With them we prove the theorem, test it on the turned plate, and say what it means for the hanging bar and for a body with a hole.

The partial derivatives of the displacement contain the strain and the rotation, \(\mat H = \ten\varepsilon + \ten\omega\) (section 1.17.5). What do the strains say about the rotation? Not its values, since the field \(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r\) has zero strains and the rotation \(\mat W\), which can be any antisymmetric matrix. How the rotation changes from point to point, though, is determined by the strains, when the displacement field has continuous second partial derivatives.

We draw the lemma on the hanging bar (figure 1.400) with two graphs. On the left graph the horizontal axis is the depth \(x\) up to the end of the bar at \(L\), and the vertical axis is the strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\). The line is \(-0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\): at \(x = 0\) it has the value \(-0{,}6\,a\,L\), at \(x = L\) zero. On the right graph the horizontal axis is the coordinate \(y\), measured from the axis of the bar, and the vertical one is the rotation \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\). The line \(-0{,}6\,a\,y\) goes through the origin and falls. The blue triangle on the left measures the slope of the strain. Its horizontal leg is \(\Delta x\), the vertical one \(0{,}6\,a\,\Delta x\), so the slope is \(0{,}6\,a\). The blue triangle on the right measures the slope of the rotation. Its horizontal leg is \(\Delta y\), and the vertical one \(-0{,}6\,a\,\Delta y\), negative because the line falls. The slope is therefore \(-0{,}6\,a\). The slopes are equal in size and opposite in sign. For the hanging bar, where \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\), the lemma below will say this: \(\partial\omega_{\mathrm{xy}} / \partial y = -\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} / \partial x\). The scales of the axes differ on the graphs. On the left graph the length of the bar, 10 m, is drawn horizontally, on the right its diameter, 10 mm. So the lines do not look equally steep.

Lemma 1.128 Derivatives of the rotation from derivatives of the strains (odvodi zasuka iz odvodov deformacij)

Let \(D\) be an open set of points, and let the components \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) of a displacement field have at every point of \(D\) partial derivatives of first and second order that are continuous at every point of \(D\). Let \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) be the components of the small strain tensor (definition 1.115) and \(\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}\) the components of the small rotation tensor (definition 1.116), where the indices \(\ix{i}\), \(\ix{j}\) and \(\ix{k}\) run over \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\), and let \(x_{\mathrm{x}} = x\), \(x_{\mathrm{y}} = y\) and \(x_{\mathrm{z}} = z\). Then at every point of \(D\), for all \(\ix{i}\), \(\ix{j}\) and \(\ix{k}\) we have:

  1. the partial derivatives of the rotation are differences of partial derivatives of the strains,
    \[\frac{\partial\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}} = \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ik}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} - \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jk}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}} , \tag{1.69}\]
  2. the second partial derivatives of the displacements are sums of partial derivatives of the strains and the rotation,
    \[\frac{\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} = \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}} + \frac{\partial\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}} = \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}} + \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ik}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} - \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jk}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}} .\]
Proof

We have to show that the two sides of both equalities agree when the components of the strain and the rotation are written with partial derivatives of the displacements. We compute partial derivatives as ordinary derivatives, so the two rules of lemma 1.81 hold for them: the derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives, and a constant factor can be taken out.

1. Derivatives of the rotation.

  1. By definition 1.116, \(\omega_{\mathrm{ij}} = \tfrac12\big(\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} - \partial u_{\mathrm{j}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\big)\). We differentiate with respect to \(x_{\mathrm{k}}\) and get, by definition 1.124,
    \[\frac{\partial\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}} = \frac12\,\frac{\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} - \frac12\,\frac{\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{j}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}} .\]
  2. By definition 1.115, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ik}} = \tfrac12\big(\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{k}} + \partial u_{\mathrm{k}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\big)\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jk}} = \tfrac12\big(\partial u_{\mathrm{j}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{k}} + \partial u_{\mathrm{k}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\big)\). We differentiate the first with respect to \(x_{\mathrm{j}}\), the second with respect to \(x_{\mathrm{i}}\), and write the difference:
    \[\frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ik}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} - \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jk}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}} = \frac12\,\frac{\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}} + \frac12\,\frac{\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{k}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}} - \frac12\,\frac{\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{j}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}} - \frac12\,\frac{\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{k}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} .\]
  3. Let \(P\) be a point of \(D\). Since \(D\) is open, all points at a distance less than some number \(r > 0\) from \(P\) are in \(D\). At them the first and second partial derivatives of the displacements exist, and at \(P\) they are continuous. So by theorem 1.125 on the symmetry of mixed partial derivatives, the order of two differentiations does not matter at \(P\). With two equal variables there is nothing to swap. In the second term on the right of step 2 we swap the order and get the same derivative as in the fourth term, with the opposite sign, so they cancel. We swap the order in the first and the third term too:
    \[\frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ik}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} - \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jk}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}} = \frac12\,\frac{\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} - \frac12\,\frac{\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{j}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}} .\]
  4. The right side is the right side of step 1, so (1.69) holds.

2. Second derivatives of the displacements.

  1. By section 1.17.5, \(\mat H = \ten\varepsilon + \ten\omega\), entry by entry \(\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} + \omega_{\mathrm{ij}}\).
  2. We differentiate both sides with respect to \(x_{\mathrm{k}}\). The derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives, so we get the first equality of item 2. We get the second when we replace \(\partial\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}\) by (1.69).

Source: SADD (2.6.6) (PDF p. 52), written with commas for partial derivatives, \(\omega_{\mathrm{ij},\mathrm{k}} = e_{\mathrm{ik},\mathrm{j}} - e_{\mathrm{jk},\mathrm{i}}\), and with the same sign of the rotation as ours (SADD (2.1.7), PDF p. 40). The proof follows the source, and we justify swapping the order of differentiation by the theorem on the symmetry of mixed partial derivatives.

Step 3 of the proof on the four terms on the right of step 2, from left to right:

term from step 2 after swapping the order of differentiation what happens to it
\(+\tfrac12\,\dfrac{\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}}\) \(+\tfrac12\,\dfrac{\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}}\) stays, the first term on the right of step 1
\(+\tfrac12\,\dfrac{\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{k}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}}\) \(+\tfrac12\,\dfrac{\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{k}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}}\) the same derivative as in the fourth term, they cancel
\(-\tfrac12\,\dfrac{\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{j}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}}\) \(-\tfrac12\,\dfrac{\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{j}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}}\) stays, the second term on the right of step 1
\(-\tfrac12\,\dfrac{\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{k}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}}\) no swap cancels with the second term

The lemma says that the rotation cannot change arbitrarily: how fast it changes in the direction of the axis \(x_{\mathrm{k}}\) is determined by derivatives of the strains. Let us test it on the hanging bar. A steel bar of length \(L = 10\) m hangs under its own weight, the axis \(x\) points vertically down from the centre \(O\) of the top end, and \(a = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1}\). From the table of partial derivatives in section 1.7.2 we have at every point

\[\omega_{\mathrm{xy}} = \frac12\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y} - \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x}\Big) = \frac12\,(-0{,}6\,a\,y - 0{,}6\,a\,y) = -0{,}6\,a\,y ,\]

with the derivative \(-0{,}6\,a\) with respect to \(y\). The lemma with \(\ix{i} = x\), \(\ix{j} = y\) and \(\ix{k} = y\) gives the same from the strains of the bar, which we computed in section 1.18.3, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\):

\[\frac{\partial\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial y} = \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial y} - \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}}{\partial x} = 0 - 0{,}6\,a = -1{,}171 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1} .\]

Figure 1.95 shows the meaning. The bar thins more at the top than at the bottom, since \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) grows with depth at the rate \(0{,}6\,a\). So the vertical fibres tilt, the more the farther from the axis they lie, and the material turns the more, the farther from the axis it is (figure 1.400). At the point \(P\), 4 mm from the axis, \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}} = -0{,}6\,a \cdot 0{,}004\ \text{m} = -4{,}685 \cdot 10^{-10}\), as in section 1.17.5.

The lemma also gives a short route to the goal of the section. If the strains are zero at every point, so are their derivatives, and by item 2 of the lemma all second partial derivatives of the displacements are zero. This route, however, needs the second partial derivatives of the displacements to exist and be continuous. In chapter 4 we will need the theorem for the difference of two displacement fields, about which we will only know that it is continuously differentiable. So we prove it with first partial derivatives only. The idea is geometric and has three steps (figure 1.401).

  1. Zero strain means that no short fibre gets longer to first order. We will show that therefore not even a long segment in the body gets longer to first order. For the segment from \(A\) to \(B\) with the vector \(\vek d = \overrightarrow{AB}\) we will have \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \big(u_{\mathrm{i}}(B) - u_{\mathrm{i}}(A)\big)\,d_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\). When we expand the square of the length of the segment after loading, as in section 1.17.5, the first-order term is twice this sum. A sum equal to zero therefore says that the segment does not get longer to first order: the difference of the displacements of the ends has no part in the direction of the segment, it is perpendicular to it. So all points of the segment move equally far along the segment, like the points of a rigid rod (grey dimensions in figure 1.401, left).
  2. In a small ball around a point \(C\) this holds for all three sides of every triangle with the corner \(C\). No side gets longer to first order, so the triangle only moves and turns. We denote the difference of displacements by \(\vek g(\vek v) = \vek u(C + \vek v) - \vek u(C)\) (blue dimensions in the figure on the right). We will derive that \(\vek g(\vek v)\) is the product of an antisymmetric matrix with the vector \(\vek v\). Let us write the way there as a series of steps of the proof:
    \[\begin{aligned} & \textstyle\sum_{\mathrm{i}} g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek w)\,v_{\mathrm{i}} = -\sum_{\mathrm{i}} g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek v)\,w_{\mathrm{i}} && \text{(korak 8)} \\ \Longrightarrow\ & \vek g(\vek v + \vek w) = \vek g(\vek v) + \vek g(\vek w) && \text{(korak 10)} \\ & \vek g(\lambda\,\vek v) = \lambda\,\vek g(\vek v) && \text{(korak 11)} \\ & \vek g(\vek v) = \mat W_{\mathrm{C}}\,\vek v && \text{(korak 12)} \\ & \mat W_{\mathrm{C}}^\T = -\mat W_{\mathrm{C}} && \text{(korak 13)} \end{aligned}\]
  3. So the displacement gradient is constant near every point. For it to be the same in the whole body we need that from every point of the body we can reach every other one along a path in the body.

Figure 1.401 has two parts. The left part shows what the proof says about a segment. The grey closed curve is the boundary of the open set \(D\), that is, the body in which the displacement field has no strains. The blackwhite segment from the point \(A\) to the point \(B\) lies in \(D\). On it are five points at equal spacing. The field \(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r\) is drawn with greatly magnified entries of the matrix \(\mat W\), so that it can be seen. The orange segment is the segment after the displacement, shifted and turned. The blue arrows are the displacements of the five points. The grey dashed vertical lines drop the end of each arrow onto the line of the segment, so that it can be seen how far the point moves in the direction of the segment. The grey dimensions below the segment reach from each point to the foot of its vertical line and are all equally long. The right part is drawn on a larger scale around the point \(C\), so that the labels do not overlap the triangle. The grey dashed circle is the ball with centre \(C\) and radius \(\rho\). The ball lies entirely in the body \(D\). The blackwhite triangle has corners \(C\), \(X = C + \vek v\) and \(Y = C + \vek w\). From \(X\) and \(Y\) lead the blue arrows, the differences of displacements \(\vek g(\vek v)\) and \(\vek g(\vek w)\) relative to \(C\). Both are perpendicular to the side that leads from \(C\) to the same point, as the grey right-angle marks show. The orange triangle is the triangle after the displacement, turned about \(C\).

What it means for a body to be in one piece, and why it matters, is shown by an example (figure 1.402). Two steel cubes with an edge of 10 mm lie on a table, separated by a gap. Let us draw this from the front. The axis \(x\) points from the left cube to the right, with coordinates in millimetres. We leave the left cube, a blackwhite square from \(0\) to \(10\) mm, in place. The right cube before the shift is a blackwhite square from \(20\) to \(30\) mm, and the right one after the shift is an orange square. We shift it as a whole by 1 mm in the direction of the axis \(x\). The blue arrows measure this shift at the left and right edge of the cube, it is the same everywhere. In the figure the shift is four times longer than it would be on the scale of the cubes, so that it can be seen. The grey segment from \(A_{\mathrm{k}-1}\) to \(A_{\mathrm{k}}\) and the empty circle above the label \(15\) belong to a broken line that we will define below, and we explain them there. The displacement field is \((0, 0, 0)\) at the points of the left cube and \((1, 0, 0)\) in millimetres at the points of the right one. Around every point the displacement is constant, so all partial derivatives and all strains are zero. But the field is not of the form \(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r\) with the same \(\vek a\) and \(\mat W\) in both cubes. If it were, then for the points \(P\) and \(P + h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\) in the left cube we would have \(\vek u(P + h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}) - \vek u(P) = \mat W\,(h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}})\). The left side is \(\vek 0\), the right side is \(h\) times the column \(\ix{j}\) of the matrix \(\mat W\) (definition 1.96). All columns would be zero, \(\mat W = \mat 0\), and from \(\vek 0 = \vek a + \mat 0\,\vek r_{\mathrm{P}}\) it would follow that \(\vek a = \vek 0\). The displacement in the right cube, though, is not \(\vek 0\). Each cube moves rigidly, but each in its own way. The theorem must therefore require the body to be in one piece, and we will state this with segments.

The segment from a point \(A\) to a point \(B\) is the set of points \(A + t\,\overrightarrow{AB}\) for the numbers \(t\) from \(0\) to \(1\). At \(t = 0\) we are at \(A\), at \(t = 1\) at \(B\) ((1.8)). How far are the points of the segment from a given point \(C\)? Let us draw this (figure 1.403). The blackwhite segment has the end points \(A\) and \(B\), its length is \(|AB|\). Outside it is the point \(C\). The point \(T\) on the segment is for \(t = 0{,}6\), which the grey dimensions below the segment show: from \(A\) to \(T\) it is \(t\,|AB|\), and from \(T\) to \(B\) it is \((1 - t)\,|AB|\). We look for the distance \(|CT|\), the blue line, expressed through the distances to the end points, the grey lines \(|CA|\) and \(|CB|\), and the length of the segment. The grey dashed circle is the ball with centre \(C\) and radius \(\rho\), in which \(A\) and \(B\) lie. Beside each line its length is written. We will need the answer for the ball in which we carry out the second step of the proof, and for the ring.

Lemma 1.129 Distance to the points of a segment (razdalja do točk daljice)

Let \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\) be points, \(t\) a number and \(T = A + t\,\overrightarrow{AB}\). Then:

  1. the square of the distance from \(C\) to \(T\) is
    \[|CT|^2 = (1 - t)\,|CA|^2 + t\,|CB|^2 - t\,(1 - t)\,|AB|^2 , \tag{1.70}\]
  2. \(t\,(1 - t) \le \tfrac14\), so \(|CT|^2 \ge (1 - t)\,|CA|^2 + t\,|CB|^2 - \tfrac14\,|AB|^2\),
  3. if \(0 \le t \le 1\) and \(A\) and \(B\) are at a distance less than some number \(\rho > 0\) from \(C\), then \(T\) is also at a distance less than \(\rho\) from \(C\).
Proof

We have to show the equality of item 1 and then get from it the inequalities of items 2 and 3.

1. The equality.

  1. The coordinate \(x\) of the point \(T\) is \(x_{\mathrm{A}} + t\,(x_{\mathrm{B}} - x_{\mathrm{A}})\) (definition 1.14). Let us draw it (figure 1.404, left): on the number line are the coordinates of the points \(C\), \(A\), \(B\) and \(T\). Let \(p = x_{\mathrm{A}} - x_{\mathrm{C}}\) and \(q = x_{\mathrm{B}} - x_{\mathrm{C}}\). Then \(x_{\mathrm{B}} - x_{\mathrm{A}} = q - p\) and \(x_{\mathrm{T}} - x_{\mathrm{C}} = p + t\,(q - p) = (1 - t)\,p + t\,q\), where \(t\,(q - p)\) is the distance from \(A\) to \(T\).
  2. We square: \((x_{\mathrm{T}} - x_{\mathrm{C}})^2 = (1 - t)^2\,p^2 + 2t\,(1 - t)\,p\,q + t^2\,q^2\).
  3. The right side of (1.70) has for the coordinate \(x\) the part
    \[(1 - t)\,p^2 + t\,q^2 - t\,(1 - t)\,(q - p)^2 .\]
    We expand the square of the difference, \((q - p)^2 = q^2 - 2p\,q + p^2\), and collect the terms with the same product:
    \[\begin{aligned} p^2 &: \quad (1 - t) - t\,(1 - t) = (1 - t)^2 , \\ q^2 &: \quad t - t\,(1 - t) = t^2 , \\ p\,q &: \quad -t\,(1 - t) \cdot (-2) = 2t\,(1 - t) . \end{aligned}\]
    This is the expression of step 2.
  4. The same holds for the coordinates \(y\) and \(z\). The square of the distance is the sum of the squares of the differences of the coordinates ((1.10)), so we add the three equalities and get (1.70).

2. Lower bound.

  1. We expand \(\tfrac14 - t\,(1 - t) = t^2 - t + \tfrac14 = \big(t - \tfrac12\big)^2\). A square is not negative, so \(t\,(1 - t) \le \tfrac14\). On the right of figure 1.404 is the graph of the function \(t\,(1 - t)\) on the axes \(t\) and \(t\,(1 - t)\), its peak at \(t = \tfrac12\) is \(\tfrac14\).
  2. The number \(|AB|^2\) is not negative, so \(t\,(1 - t)\,|AB|^2 \le \tfrac14\,|AB|^2\): the largest value \(\tfrac14\) from the figure, multiplied by \(|AB|^2\). Putting this into (1.70) gives the inequality of item 2.

3. A point in the ball.

  1. For \(0 \le t \le 1\) the point \(T\) lies between \(A\) and \(B\), the numbers \(t\) and \(1 - t\) are not negative, so the last term in (1.70) is not positive, and \(|CT|^2 \le (1 - t)\,|CA|^2 + t\,|CB|^2\).
  2. By the assumption and by lemma 1.28 that a larger nonnegative number has a larger square, \(|CA|^2 < \rho^2\) and \(|CB|^2 < \rho^2\). The numbers \(1 - t\) and \(t\) are not negative and at least one of them is positive, so \((1 - t)\,|CA|^2 + t\,|CB|^2 < (1 - t)\,\rho^2 + t\,\rho^2 = \rho^2\).
  3. By steps 1 and 2, \(|CT|^2 < \rho^2\), and by the same lemma \(|CT| < \rho\).

Source: The lemma is not from a source.

Item 3 says that a ball, that is, the set of all points at a distance less than \(\rho\) from a point \(C\), contains together with every two of its points also the segment between them. Item 1 says something more about a circle. If \(A\) and \(B\) are different points at the distance \(\rho\) from \(C\), then for \(0 < t < 1\) the distance \(|CT|^2 = \rho^2 - t\,(1 - t)\,|AB|^2\) is smaller than \(\rho^2\). All points of the segment between them are therefore closer to \(C\) than \(\rho\), and none except the ends lies on the circle or the sphere of radius \(\rho\).

Now we can state when a set is in one piece. We want to get from point to point along a path of straight pieces that does not leave the set.

Definition 1.130 Connected open set (povezana odprta množica)

A broken line (lomljena črta) from a point \(P\) to a point \(Q\) is a sequence of finitely many points \(P = A_0, A_1, \dots, A_{\mathrm{m}} = Q\) together with the segments \(A_0 A_1\), \(A_1 A_2\), ..., \(A_{\mathrm{m}-1} A_{\mathrm{m}}\), where the segment \(AB\) is the set of points \(A + t\,\overrightarrow{AB}\) with \(0 \le t \le 1\). An open set of points \(D\) is connected (povezana) if every two of its points \(P\) and \(Q\) can be joined by a broken line that lies entirely in \(D\).

Source: KREYSZIG §9.6 (PDF p. 419), where this explains what a connected open set in space means, and KREYSZIG §13.3 (PDF p. 646) for sets in the plane.

This is one form of the general notion of connectedness (LEBL1 Def. 7.2.13 and Prop. 7.2.14, PDF p. 268), which for open sets in space is equivalent to the general one. We will use only this form. It suits only open sets, though. On a circle, for example, by item 1 of lemma 1.129 no segment with two different ends lies, so two of its points cannot be joined by a broken line in the circle, although the circle is in one piece.

Which bodies are connected? If a set contains together with every two points also the segment between them, a broken line of a single segment is enough. This is so for a ball by item 3 of lemma 1.129. It is so for a box with edges along the axes, because the coordinate \(x_{\mathrm{A}} + t\,(x_{\mathrm{B}} - x_{\mathrm{A}})\) of a point of the segment lies between \(x_{\mathrm{A}}\) and \(x_{\mathrm{B}}\) for \(0 \le t \le 1\), and likewise for \(y\) and \(z\). It is also so for a cylinder with axis \(x\), for example the round hanging bar. The coordinate \(x\) of a point of the segment lies between the coordinates of the ends, and for the distance from the axis we use item 3 of the lemma on the points \((0, y_{\mathrm{A}}, z_{\mathrm{A}})\), \((0, y_{\mathrm{B}}, z_{\mathrm{B}})\) and \(C = O\).

The two separate cubes of figure 1.402 are not connected. The left cube reaches from \(x = 0\) to \(x = 10\) mm, the right one from \(x = 20\) mm to \(x = 30\) mm (coordinates on the axis \(x\)). All corners of a broken line in the set lie in one of the cubes. If the line starts in the left cube and ends in the right one, the first corner \(A_{\mathrm{k}}\) in the right cube has before it a corner \(A_{\mathrm{k}-1}\) in the left one (the grey segment between them). On this segment, with \(A = A_{\mathrm{k}-1}\) and \(B = A_{\mathrm{k}}\), the coordinate \(x_{\mathrm{A}} + t\,(x_{\mathrm{B}} - x_{\mathrm{A}})\) goes from less than \(10\) mm to more than \(20\) mm and equals \(15\) mm at some \(t\). The point with this coordinate is the empty circle, which the grey dashed line drops to the axis at \(15\) mm. It is empty because the point is in neither cube.

A body with a hole, though, can be connected too. Such is the ring, the simplest body with a hole (figure 1.405). In the next section we will show that in a body with a hole the compatibility equations are not enough: the ring will have strains that satisfy them at every point, and no displacement field. We will cut the ring from the inner to the outer edge, and the cut ring will accept the prescribed strains by the cut opening. That the slit cannot close will follow from the strains determining the displacements of the cut ring up to a rigid motion. We prove this in this section only for connected bodies. If the cut ring were not connected, its parts could move each in its own way, like the two cubes above, and the slit could close. So we prove the connectedness of the cut ring now, together with the connectedness of the whole ring, which we need in chapter 4.

Let us draw the ring. Both parts of the figure show the ring from above. The two blackwhite circles are its inner edge with radius 40 mm and its outer edge with radius 60 mm, the point \(O\) is the common centre. The grey dashed circle with radius 50 mm lies in the middle of the ring. On it are seven grey dots \(K_2\) to \(K_8\), of the eight points \(K_1\) to \(K_8\), which are all \(50\) mm from \(O\), beside the axes and at the coordinates \(30\) and \(40\) mm. \(K_1\) is on the cut and is not drawn. The six grey segments between them are six of the eight sides of the octagon \(K_1 K_2 \dots K_8\), which lies in the ring. The sides \(K_8 K_1\) and \(K_1 K_2\) are not drawn, because they touch the cut, since \(K_1\) lies on it. The thick grey line is the cut, which goes along the positive axis \(x\) from the inner to the outer edge. On the right the ring is cut. On the left the ring is whole, and the thick line there only marks the points that the cut ring does not have. On the right we draw how we join the points \(P\) and \(Q\) of the cut ring. The blue broken line goes from \(P\) along a ray from \(O\) to the point \(M\) on the middle circle and then straight to \(K_2\). From there it goes along the sides of the octagon to \(K_7\), straight to the middle circle on the ray from \(O\) through \(Q\), and along this ray to \(Q\). It touches the cut nowhere. In the left figure \(P\) and \(M\) are other points than on the right, but \(Q\) is the same. The left \(P\) is on the cut, so not in the cut ring. The small grey dashed circle around it is a ball that lies entirely in the ring. The point \(P'\) in it is above \(P\) by half of the radius of the ball, so it is in the cut ring. From there the blue line goes along a ray to \(M\) on the middle circle, straight to \(K_2\) and from there along the same route as on the right to \(Q\).

Lemma 1.131 The ring is connected (obroč je povezan)

Lengths are measured in millimetres, \(c > 0\) is a number, and \(\rho_{\mathrm{P}} = \sqrt{x_{\mathrm{P}}^2 + y_{\mathrm{P}}^2}\) is the distance of a point \(P\) from the axis \(z\). Let the ring be the set of points \(P\) with \(40 < \rho_{\mathrm{P}} < 60\) and \(|z_{\mathrm{P}}| < c\), and the cut ring the ring without the points with \(y_{\mathrm{P}} = 0\) and \(x_{\mathrm{P}} > 0\). Then both sets are open and connected (definition 1.130).

Proof

We have to show that every point of both sets is an interior point and that every two points can be joined by a broken line in the set. First we join the points of the cut ring, where we avoid the cut, and then the points on the cut. We will use eight points on the circle of radius \(50\) in the plane \(z = 0\),

\[\begin{aligned} K_1 &= (50, 0, 0) , & K_2 &= (30, 40, 0) , & K_3 &= (0, 50, 0) , \\ K_4 &= (-30, 40, 0) , & K_5 &= (-50, 0, 0) , & K_6 &= (-30, -40, 0) , \\ K_7 &= (0, -50, 0) , & K_8 &= (30, -40, 0) , \end{aligned}\]

for which \(30^2 + 40^2 = 50^2\) (figure 1.405).

1. Both sets are open.

  1. The functions \(f(Q) = x_{\mathrm{Q}}^2 + y_{\mathrm{Q}}^2\) and \(z_{\mathrm{Q}}\) are polynomials in the coordinates, so they are continuous at every point (corollary 1.69 on the continuity of sums, products and polynomials in space, item 2). So are the coordinates \(x_{\mathrm{Q}}\) and \(y_{\mathrm{Q}}\).
  2. Let \(P\) be a point of the ring. By lemma 1.28, \(1600 < f(P) < 3600\). Let \(\eta\) be the smallest of the positive numbers \(f(P) - 1600\), \(3600 - f(P)\) and \(c - |z_{\mathrm{P}}|\). By the definition of continuity 1.67 there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that for every point \(Q\) with \(|PQ| < \delta\) the values \(f(Q)\) and \(z_{\mathrm{Q}}\) differ from \(f(P)\) and \(z_{\mathrm{P}}\) by less than \(\eta\).
  3. For such a point, \(1600 < f(Q) < 3600\), so \(40 < \rho_{\mathrm{Q}} < 60\), and by the triangle inequality for numbers \(|z_{\mathrm{Q}}| \le |z_{\mathrm{P}}| + |z_{\mathrm{Q}} - z_{\mathrm{P}}| < c\). The point \(Q\) is in the ring, so \(P\) is an interior point of the ring.
  4. For a point \(P\) of the cut ring we also reduce \(\eta\) to \(|y_{\mathrm{P}}|\) if \(y_{\mathrm{P}} \neq 0\), and otherwise to \(|x_{\mathrm{P}}|\), since then \(x_{\mathrm{P}} < 0\). We choose the number \(\delta\) for this \(\eta\) so that at the points \(Q\) with \(|PQ| < \delta\) also the coordinates \(x_{\mathrm{Q}}\) and \(y_{\mathrm{Q}}\) differ from \(x_{\mathrm{P}}\) and \(y_{\mathrm{P}}\) by less than \(\eta\) (step 1). The points \(Q\) with \(|PQ| < \delta\) then have \(y_{\mathrm{Q}}\) of the same sign as \(y_{\mathrm{P}}\), or else \(x_{\mathrm{Q}} < 0\), so they are not on the cut.

2. The cut ring and the ring are connected.

  1. From a point \(P\) of the cut ring we go straight to the point \(M\) \(= \lambda_1\,(x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}}, 0)\) with \(\lambda_1 = 50/\rho_{\mathrm{P}}\), which lies on the circle of radius \(50\) in the plane \(z = 0\). The points of this segment are \(\big(\lambda\,x_{\mathrm{P}},\ \lambda\,y_{\mathrm{P}},\ (1 - t)\,z_{\mathrm{P}}\big)\) with \(\lambda = (1 - t) + t\,\lambda_1 > 0\). Their distance from the axis \(z\) is \(\lambda\,\rho_{\mathrm{P}} = (1 - t)\,\rho_{\mathrm{P}} + 50\,t\) and lies between \(\rho_{\mathrm{P}}\) and \(50\), and \(|(1 - t)\,z_{\mathrm{P}}| \le |z_{\mathrm{P}}| < c\), so they are in the ring. The coordinates \(x\) and \(y\) are multiplied by the positive number \(\lambda\) and keep their signs, so the segment does not meet the cut.
  2. Let \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) be points in the plane \(z = 0\) at the distance \(50\) from \(O\), with \(|M_1 M_2|^2 < 3600\). For a point \(T\) of the segment between them, by items 1 and 2 of lemma 1.129 with \(C = O\),
    \[2500 - \tfrac14\,|M_1 M_2|^2 \le |OT|^2 \le 2500 ,\]
    so \(1600 < |OT|^2 \le 2500\). The point \(T\) lies in the plane \(z = 0\), so \(|OT| = \rho_{\mathrm{T}}\), and \(40 < \rho_{\mathrm{T}} \le 50\). The segment lies in the ring.
  3. The squares of the distances between consecutive points \(K_1, K_2, \dots, K_8, K_1\) are \(2000\) or \(1000\), for example \(|K_1 K_2|^2 = 20^2 + 40^2 = 2000\) and \(|K_2 K_3|^2 = 30^2 + 10^2 = 1000\). By step 2 all these segments are in the ring. A coordinate of a point of a segment lies between the coordinates of the ends. The segments \(K_2 K_3\) and \(K_3 K_4\) therefore have \(y > 0\) everywhere, the segments \(K_4 K_5\) and \(K_5 K_6\) have \(x < 0\) everywhere, and the segments \(K_6 K_7\) and \(K_7 K_8\) have \(y < 0\) everywhere. The broken line \(K_2, K_3, \dots, K_8\) is therefore in the cut ring, since it does not touch the cut.
  4. Let \(M\) be a point of the cut ring on the circle of radius \(50\) in the plane \(z = 0\), as in step 1. Either \(|x_{\mathrm{M}}| \ge |y_{\mathrm{M}}|\) or \(|y_{\mathrm{M}}| \ge |x_{\mathrm{M}}|\). Let first \(x_{\mathrm{M}} \ge |y_{\mathrm{M}}|\). Then \(2x_{\mathrm{M}}^2 \ge x_{\mathrm{M}}^2 + y_{\mathrm{M}}^2 = 2500\), so \(x_{\mathrm{M}}^2 \ge 1250 > 35^2\) and \(x_{\mathrm{M}} > 35\). The point \(M\) is not on the cut, so \(y_{\mathrm{M}} \neq 0\). Since \(M\) lies on the circle of radius \(50\), \(x_{\mathrm{M}}^2 + y_{\mathrm{M}}^2 = 2500\), and we use this when we expand the squares: \((x_{\mathrm{M}} - 30)^2 + (y_{\mathrm{M}} - 40)^2 = x_{\mathrm{M}}^2 + y_{\mathrm{M}}^2 - 60\,x_{\mathrm{M}} - 80\,y_{\mathrm{M}} + 2500\). For \(y_{\mathrm{M}} > 0\) we join it to \(K_2\):
    \[\begin{aligned} |M K_2|^2 &= (x_{\mathrm{M}} - 30)^2 + (y_{\mathrm{M}} - 40)^2 = 5000 - 60\,x_{\mathrm{M}} - 80\,y_{\mathrm{M}} \\ &< 5000 - 60 \cdot 35 = 2900 , \end{aligned}\]
    and for \(y_{\mathrm{M}} < 0\) to \(K_8\), where \(|M K_8|^2 = 5000 - 60\,x_{\mathrm{M}} + 80\,y_{\mathrm{M}} < 2900\). By step 2 the segment lies in the ring, and since both ends have \(y > 0\) or both have \(y < 0\), the whole segment has that sign, so it does not meet the cut. For \(y_{\mathrm{M}} \ge |x_{\mathrm{M}}|\) we have \(y_{\mathrm{M}} > 35\) and \(|M K_3|^2 = 5000 - 100\,y_{\mathrm{M}} < 1500\), and the segment has \(y > 0\) everywhere. Likewise the segments to \(K_5\) and to \(K_7\) in the other two cases, \(-x_{\mathrm{M}} \ge |y_{\mathrm{M}}|\) and \(-y_{\mathrm{M}} \ge |x_{\mathrm{M}}|\), are in the ring and have \(x < 0\) and \(y < 0\) everywhere.
  5. For points \(P\) and \(Q\) of the cut ring we put together a broken line from step 1 from \(P\) to \(M_{\mathrm{P}}\), from step 4 from \(M_{\mathrm{P}}\) to one of the points \(K_2, \dots, K_8\), by step 3 to the point \(K_{\mathrm{j}}\) that belongs to the point \(Q\), and from steps 4 and 1 in reverse order to \(Q\) (the blue broken line in figure 1.405, right). The cut ring is connected.
  6. Let \(P\) be a point of the ring. If \(P\) is not on the cut, it is in the cut ring. If it is on the cut, by part 1 there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that all points with \(|PQ| < \delta\) are in the ring (the small ball in the figure on the left), among them \(P' = P + (0, \delta/2, 0)\) with \(y_{\mathrm{P}'} > 0\). The segment \(PP'\) is in the ring, because its points are at most \(\delta/2\) from \(P\), and \(P'\) is in the cut ring. So every point of the ring is joined to the cut ring by a short segment or by none, and in the cut ring step 5 applies. The ring is connected.

Source: The lemma is not from a source.

Figure 1.406 has two parts. On the left is the plane, seen from above. The grey region is the open set \(D\). The segment goes from the point \(P\) to the point \(P + \vek d\), the vector \(\vek d\) above it is its direction and length. The point \(S = P + t\,\vek d\) is on the segment, the ball around it is the grey dashed circle, which stays in \(D\) because \(D\) is open. The point \(Q\) is a step \(s\,\vek d\) ahead of \(S\), so \(Q = P + (t + s)\,\vek d\). Drawn are \(t = 0{,}4\) and \(s = 0{,}3\). The step is shorter than the radius of the ball, so \(Q\) lies in it. On the right is the function of one variable \(g(t)\) along the segment. The horizontal axis is \(t\), which shows where on the segment we are, and the vertical axis is the value of the function. The blackwhite curve is \(g\). The grey dashed vertical lines and labels show the values \(t\) and \(t + s\), the same as on the left, and the dots the corresponding points on the curve, \(g(t) = f(S)\) and \(g(t + s) = f(Q)\). The blue line is the tangent at the point at \(t\). We denote its slope by \(m\). The proof below will write \(m\) with the partial derivatives of \(f\) at \(S\) and show that this really is the slope of the tangent, \(g'(t)\). The blue dimension \(m\,s\) is by how much the tangent rises over the step \(s\), and the orange dimension \(R\) is the remainder: by that much the curve at \(t + s\) exceeds the tangent.

Now we need one more tool, for the first step of the proof. Along the segment from \(P\) in the direction of the vector \(\vek d\), like the segment from \(A\) to \(B\) in figure 1.401, a field is a function of one variable \(t\), which tells where on the segment we are (figure 1.406). For a step along an axis its derivative was a partial derivative (lemma 1.87 on the change over a step along an axis). In an arbitrary direction we expect, as in corollary 1.92 on the difference of displacements along a fibre, the sum of products of the partial derivatives with the components of the direction.

Lemma 1.132 Derivative along a segment (odvod vzdolž daljice)

Let \(D\) be an open set of points and \(f\) a function of three variables that is continuously differentiable on \(D\) (definition 1.90). Let \(P\) be a point and \(\vek d = (d_{\mathrm{x}}, d_{\mathrm{y}}, d_{\mathrm{z}})\) a vector. For every number \(t\) for which the point \(P + t\,\vek d\) is in \(D\), let \(g(t) = f(P + t\,\vek d)\). Then for every such number \(t\):

  1. the function \(g\) is defined at all numbers at a distance less than some positive number from \(t\), and it is differentiable at \(t\) with the derivative
    \[\begin{aligned} g'(t) &= \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}}(P + t\,\vek d)\,d_{\mathrm{j}} \\ &= \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(P + t\,\vek d)\,d_{\mathrm{x}} + \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(P + t\,\vek d)\,d_{\mathrm{y}} \\ &\quad + \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}(P + t\,\vek d)\,d_{\mathrm{z}} , \end{aligned} \tag{1.71}\]
  2. the derivative \(g'\) is continuous at \(t\).
Proof

We have to show that the derivative exists, its value, and its continuity. Let \(t\) be a number for which \(S = P + t\,\vek d\) is in \(D\).

1. The derivative.

  1. If \(\vek d = \vek 0\), then \(g\) is the constant function with the value \(f(P)\), defined for all numbers. By lemma 1.81 on the rules of differentiation, item 4, its derivative is \(0\), which is also the right side of (1.71). From now on let \(\vek d \neq \vek 0\).
  2. Since \(D\) is open, there is an \(r > 0\) such that all points at a distance less than \(r\) from \(S\) are in \(D\). The point \(P + (t + s)\,\vek d = S + s\,\vek d\) is at the distance \(\sqrt{s^2 d_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + s^2 d_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + s^2 d_{\mathrm{z}}^2} = |s|\,|\vek d|\) from \(S\) ((1.10)). For \(|s| < r/|\vek d|\) it is therefore in \(D\), and \(g\) is defined at all numbers \(t + s\) with \(|s| < r/|\vek d|\).
  3. Let \(0 < |s| < r/|\vek d|\) and \(Q = S + s\,\vek d\). The components of the step from \(S\) to \(Q\) are \(s\,d_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(s\,d_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(s\,d_{\mathrm{z}}\). The function \(f\) is defined at all points at a distance less than \(r\) from \(S\), its partial derivatives exist there and are continuous at \(S\), so theorem 1.88 on the change of a field over a short step holds. By (1.34),
    \[g(t + s) - g(t) = f(Q) - f(S) = m\,s + R(Q) , \qquad m = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}}(S)\,d_{\mathrm{j}} .\]
  4. We divide by \(s\). The difference quotient of the function \(g\) at \(t\) is \(m + R(Q)/s\).
  5. We pick any error \(\eta > 0\). By the theorem on the change of a field with the error \(\eta/(2|\vek d|)\) there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that \(|R(Q)| \le \tfrac{\eta}{2|\vek d|}\,|SQ|\) for every point \(Q\) with \(0 < |SQ| < \delta\). Let \(\delta'\) be smaller than the numbers \(\delta/|\vek d|\) and \(r/|\vek d|\). For \(0 < |s| < \delta'\) we have \(0 < |SQ| = |s|\,|\vek d| < \delta\), so
    \[\Big|\frac{g(t + s) - g(t)}{s} - m\Big| = \frac{|R(Q)|}{|s|} \le \frac{\eta}{2|\vek d|} \cdot \frac{|s|\,|\vek d|}{|s|} = \frac{\eta}{2} < \eta .\]
  6. By the definition of the limit 1.5 the limit of the difference quotient is equal to \(m\). By the definition of the derivative 1.9, \(g\) is differentiable at \(t\) and \(g'(t) = m\), which is (1.71).

2. Continuity of the derivative.

  1. For \(\vek d = \vek 0\) the derivative \(g'\) is zero everywhere and therefore continuous. Let \(\vek d \neq \vek 0\). By step 2 of the first part all numbers \(t + s\) with \(|s| < r/|\vek d|\) are such that \(P + (t + s)\,\vek d\) is in \(D\), so by the first part \(g'\) is defined at all of them.
  2. We pick any error \(\eta > 0\). The partial derivatives of \(f\) are continuous at \(S\), so by definition 1.67 there are bands \(\delta_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\delta_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\delta_{\mathrm{z}}\) for the error \(\eta/(3|\vek d|)\). Let \(\delta'\) be the smallest of the numbers \(\delta_{\mathrm{x}}/|\vek d|\), \(\delta_{\mathrm{y}}/|\vek d|\), \(\delta_{\mathrm{z}}/|\vek d|\) and \(r/|\vek d|\).
  3. For \(|s| < \delta'\) the point \(S + s\,\vek d\) is at the distance \(|s|\,|\vek d|\) from \(S\), which is less than all three bands. Each partial derivative at it differs from its value at \(S\) by less than \(\eta/(3|\vek d|)\).
  4. No component of a vector is longer than the vector, \(|d_{\mathrm{j}}| \le |\vek d|\) (as in step 4 of the proof of theorem 1.88). By the triangle inequality for numbers and by step 3,
    \[\begin{aligned} |g'(t + s) - g'(t)| &\le \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \Big|\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}}(S + s\,\vek d) - \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}}(S)\Big|\,|d_{\mathrm{j}}| \\ &< 3 \cdot \frac{\eta}{3|\vek d|} \cdot |\vek d| = \eta . \end{aligned}\]
    The difference of the values of \(g'\) is therefore less than \(\eta\).
  5. We picked the error \(\eta\) arbitrarily and found a band \(\delta'\) for it, so by definition 1.58 the derivative \(g'\) is continuous at \(t\).

Source: LEBL2 §8.3 (PDF pp. 41-42) for the directional derivative of a differentiable function, and Prop. 8.4.6 (PDF pp. 48-49), which shows that a function with continuous partial derivatives is differentiable. The proof from the theorem on the change of a field over a short step is not from the source.

For \(\vek d = \vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) the sum in (1.71) is the partial derivative with respect to \(y\), as in the lemma on the change over a step along an axis. Now let us show that a function without change in any direction is constant on a connected set, just as for the bar a function with zero derivative is constant on an interval.

Figure 1.407 has three parts. On the left is the plane, seen from above. The grey closed curve is the boundary of the connected open set \(D\), and the blackwhite segment from \(A\) to \(B\) lies in it. In the middle is the function \(g(t) = f(A + t\,\vek d)\) along this segment, for \(t\) from \(0\) to \(1\). The axes are \(t\) and \(g\), the horizontal blackwhite line is the graph of \(g\), horizontal because the derivative is zero. The dots are the values at \(t = 0\) and \(t = 1\), and the grey dashed line shows that they are equal, \(f(A) = f(B)\). On the right is the partial derivative \(\partial f/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\) with a vertical axis and the axis of the variable. The blackwhite line is its graph, everywhere at zero. The grey dashed lines bound a band of width \(2\eta\) around zero, and the line lies in the band, however narrow it is.

Lemma 1.133 Zero partial derivatives on a connected set (ničelni parcialni odvodi na povezani množici)

Let \(D\) be a connected open set (definition 1.130) and \(f\) a function of three variables defined on \(D\) whose partial derivatives \(\partial f/\partial x\), \(\partial f/\partial y\) and \(\partial f/\partial z\) exist and are equal to zero at every point of \(D\). Then \(f\) is constant on \(D\): \(f(Q) = f(P)\) for every two points \(P\) and \(Q\) of \(D\).

Proof

We have to show that \(f\) does not change along any segment in \(D\), and carry this over to broken lines.

  1. The function \(f\) is continuously differentiable on \(D\). Its partial derivatives exist at every point of \(D\) and are zero, and the function that is zero everywhere is continuous, since the difference of its values is always \(0\), less than any error \(\eta\).
  2. Let \(A\) and \(B\) be points for which the segment \(AB\) lies in \(D\), and \(\vek d = \overrightarrow{AB}\). Let \(g(t) = f(A + t\,\vek d)\) for every \(t\) for which \(A + t\,\vek d\) is in \(D\), among them all \(t\) with \(0 \le t \le 1\). By lemma 1.132 on the derivative along a segment, item 1, for every such \(t\) the function \(g\) is defined at all numbers near \(t\), differentiable at \(t\), and \(g'(t) = 0 \cdot d_{\mathrm{x}} + 0 \cdot d_{\mathrm{y}} + 0 \cdot d_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\).
  3. By lemma 1.79 that a differentiable function is continuous, \(g\) is continuous at every \(t\) with \(0 \le t \le 1\). The condition of continuity on the interval \([0, 1]\) checks only numbers of this interval, so \(g\) is continuous on \([0, 1]\) (as in step 4 of the proof of lemma 1.87).
  4. By corollary 1.85 on a function with zero derivative, \(g(1) = g(0)\), that is, \(f(B) = f(A)\).
  5. Let \(P\) and \(Q\) be points of \(D\). By definition 1.130 there is a broken line, like the blue line in figure 1.405, \(P = A_0, A_1, \dots, A_{\mathrm{m}} = Q\) whose segments lie in \(D\). By step 4, \(f(A_{\mathrm{k}}) = f(A_{\mathrm{k}-1})\) for every \(k\) from \(1\) to \(m\), so \(f(Q) = f(A_{\mathrm{m}}) = f(A_{\mathrm{m}-1}) = \dots = f(A_0) = f(P)\).

Source: LEBL2 Cor. 8.4.4 (PDF p. 47), for connected open sets in the general sense, with a different proof. The proof with a broken line is not from the source.

Now we have everything for the theorem. Its proof follows the idea of figure 1.401: first a segment, then a triangle in a ball, and finally broken lines across the whole body. Figure 1.408 shows steps 9 to 15 of the proof, in which we get the matrix from perpendicularity along segments.

Figure 1.408 has four parts, all drawn on the field \(\vek g(\vek v) = \mat W\vek v\) with an antisymmetric matrix with the entries \(W_{\mathrm{xy}} = -s\), \(W_{\mathrm{yx}} = s\). Top left is the sum. The blackwhite vectors \(\vek v\) and \(\vek w\) lead from the point \(C\), the blue arrows are the differences of displacements at their ends and at the end of the sum \(\vek v + \vek w\). The orange dashed path lays \(\vek g(\vek v)\) and \(\vek g(\vek w)\) one after the other at the end of the sum and ends where \(\vek g(\vek v + \vek w)\) ends. Top right is the multiple. The point \(\lambda\,\vek v\) lies on the same ray from \(C\) as \(\vek v\), its displacement is \(\lambda\) times longer and points in the same direction. Bottom left is the matrix. The blackwhite segments \(h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) lie along the axes, the blue arrows at their ends are \(\vek g(h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}})\) and \(\vek g(h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}})\), equally long, one up and the other to the left, which is the antisymmetry. The vector \(\vek v\) is the sum of the parts along the axes, its displacement is the sum of the corresponding multiples of these two arrows. Bottom right are the balls around \(C\). The grey dashed circle has radius \(\rho\), the blue shaded disc has radius \(\rho/4\), and in it \(\mat H\) equals \(\mat W_{\mathrm{C}}\). The point \(X\) is in it, the grey dashed circle around it has radius \(\rho/4\) and still lies in the ball of radius \(\rho\). The blue step is \(\Delta\,\vek e_{\mathrm{k}}\) from the point \(C\).

Theorem 1.134 A displacement field without strain (polje brez deformacij)

Let \(D\) be a connected open set of points (definition 1.130) and \(\vek u\) a displacement field that is continuously differentiable on \(D\) (definition 1.90). For a point \(P\) let \(\vek r_{\mathrm{P}} = \overrightarrow{OP} = (x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}}, z_{\mathrm{P}})\) be the vector from the origin \(O\) to \(P\). Then:

  1. if the small strain tensor of the field \(\vek u\) (definition 1.115) is the zero matrix at every point of \(D\), there are a constant vector \(\vek a\) and a constant antisymmetric matrix \(\mat W\) such that
    \[\vek u(P) = \vek a + \mat W\,\vek r_{\mathrm{P}} \qquad \text{za vsako točko } P \text{ iz } D , \tag{1.72}\]
  2. conversely, every field of the form (1.72) with a constant vector \(\vek a\) and a constant antisymmetric matrix \(\mat W\) has at every point the displacement gradient \(\mat W\) and a zero small strain tensor.
Proof

We have to show that zero strains give the form (1.72), and conversely. The indices \(\ix{i}\), \(\ix{j}\) and \(\ix{k}\) run over \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\), \(x_{\mathrm{x}} = x\), \(x_{\mathrm{y}} = y\), \(x_{\mathrm{z}} = z\), and \(H_{\mathrm{ij}}(P) = \partial u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\,(P)\) are the entries of the displacement gradient \(\mat H(P)\) at the point \(P\) (definition 1.109).

1. Zero strains give the form (1.72).

  1. A segment in \(D\). Let \(A\) and \(B\) be points for which the segment \(AB\) lies in \(D\), and \(\vek d = \overrightarrow{AB}\). For every \(t\) for which \(A + t\,\vek d\) is in \(D\), let \(\varphi(t) = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} u_{\mathrm{i}}(A + t\,\vek d)\,d_{\mathrm{i}}\).
  2. By lemma 1.132 on the derivative along a segment, item 1, used for each component \(u_{\mathrm{i}}\), and by the rules for the derivative of a sum and of a multiple (lemma 1.81), for every \(t\) with \(0 \le t \le 1\) the function \(\varphi\) is defined at all numbers near \(t\), differentiable at \(t\), and
    \[\varphi'(t) = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} d_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} H_{\mathrm{ij}}(A + t\,\vek d)\,d_{\mathrm{j}} = \vek d^\T\,\mat H(A + t\,\vek d)\,\vek d ,\]
    where we wrote the double sum by (1.41).
  3. By corollary 1.104 on the double sum and the antisymmetric part, item 2, \(\vek d^\T\mat H\,\vek d = \vek d^\T\ten\varepsilon\,\vek d\), where \(\ten\varepsilon = \tfrac12(\mat H + \mat H^\T)\) is the small strain tensor. It is zero at the point \(A + t\,\vek d\), which lies in \(D\). So \(\varphi'(t) = 0\) for every \(t\) with \(0 \le t \le 1\).
  4. As in steps 3 and 4 of the proof of lemma 1.133, \(\varphi\) is continuous on \([0, 1]\) and \(\varphi(1) = \varphi(0)\) (corollary 1.85). Putting in \(\varphi(1) = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} u_{\mathrm{i}}(B)\,d_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(\varphi(0) = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} u_{\mathrm{i}}(A)\,d_{\mathrm{i}}\) we get
    \[\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \big(u_{\mathrm{i}}(B) - u_{\mathrm{i}}(A)\big)\,d_{\mathrm{i}} = 0 . \tag{1.73}\]
  5. A ball. Let \(C\) be a point of \(D\). Since \(D\) is open, there is a number \(\rho > 0\) such that all points at a distance less than \(\rho\) from \(C\) are in \(D\). For a vector \(\vek v\) with \(|\vek v| < \rho\) the point \(C + \vek v\) is at the distance \(|\vek v|\) from \(C\), so it is in \(D\). Let \(\vek g(\vek v) = \vek u(C + \vek v) - \vek u(C)\), with the components \(g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek v)\).
  6. Let \(\vek v\) and \(\vek w\) be vectors with \(|\vek v| < \rho\) and \(|\vek w| < \rho\), \(X = C + \vek v\) and \(Y = C + \vek w\). The points \(C\), \(X\) and \(Y\) are at a distance less than \(\rho\) from \(C\), so by lemma 1.129 on the distance to the points of a segment, item 3, the segments \(CX\), \(CY\) and \(XY\) lie in the ball and hence in \(D\).
  7. For the segment from \(C\) to \(X\), \(\vek d = \vek v\) and \(\vek u(X) - \vek u(C) = \vek g(\vek v)\). By (1.73), \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek v)\,v_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\): \(\vek g(\vek v)\) has no part in the direction of \(\vek v\), it is perpendicular to it. Likewise \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek w)\,w_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\) (\(\vek g(\vek w)\)).
  8. For the segment from \(X\) to \(Y\), \(\vek d = \vek w - \vek v\) and \(\vek u(Y) - \vek u(X) = [\vek g(\vek w) - \vek g(\vek v)](@fig-pbd-daljica:gv,gw)\). By (1.73), \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \big(g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek w) - g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek v)\big)(w_{\mathrm{i}} - v_{\mathrm{i}}) = 0\). We expand into four sums, \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek w)\,w_{\mathrm{i}} - \sum_{\mathrm{i}} g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek w)\,v_{\mathrm{i}} - \sum_{\mathrm{i}} g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek v)\,w_{\mathrm{i}} + \sum_{\mathrm{i}} g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek v)\,v_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\). The first and the last are zero by step 7, so
    \[\sum_{\mathrm{i}} g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek w)\,v_{\mathrm{i}} = -\sum_{\mathrm{i}} g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek v)\,w_{\mathrm{i}} . \tag{1.74}\]
  9. A sum. Let \(\vek v\), \(\vek w\) and \(\vek v + \vek w\) be shorter than \(\rho\), and let \(\vek m\) be any vector with \(|\vek m| < \rho\). By (1.74), used three times,
    \[\begin{aligned} \sum_{\mathrm{i}} g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek v + \vek w)\,m_{\mathrm{i}} &= -\sum_{\mathrm{i}} g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek m)\,(v_{\mathrm{i}} + w_{\mathrm{i}}) \\ &= -\sum_{\mathrm{i}} g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek m)\,v_{\mathrm{i}} - \sum_{\mathrm{i}} g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek m)\,w_{\mathrm{i}} \\ &= \sum_{\mathrm{i}} g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek v)\,m_{\mathrm{i}} + \sum_{\mathrm{i}} g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek w)\,m_{\mathrm{i}} , \end{aligned}\]
    so \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \big(g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek v + \vek w) - g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek v) - g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek w)\big)\,m_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\).
  10. Let \(h = \rho/2\). For \(\vek m = h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) only the term with \(\ix{i} = x\) in the sum of step 9 is nonzero, so \(h\,\big(g_{\mathrm{x}}(\vek v + \vek w) - g_{\mathrm{x}}(\vek v) - g_{\mathrm{x}}(\vek w)\big) = 0\), and the bracket is zero. Likewise with \(h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\). So \(\vek g(\vek v + \vek w) = \vek g(\vek v) + \vek g(\vek w)\).
  11. A multiple. Let \(\vek v\) be shorter than \(\rho\) and \(\lambda\) a number for which \(\lambda\,\vek v\) is also shorter than \(\rho\). By (1.74), used twice, for every \(\vek m\) with \(|\vek m| < \rho\)
    \[\sum_{\mathrm{i}} g_{\mathrm{i}}(\lambda\,\vek v)\,m_{\mathrm{i}} = -\sum_{\mathrm{i}} g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek m)\,\lambda\,v_{\mathrm{i}} = \lambda \sum_{\mathrm{i}} g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek v)\,m_{\mathrm{i}} .\]
    With \(\vek m = h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) as in step 10 we get \(\vek g(\lambda\,\vek v) = \lambda\,\vek g(\vek v)\).
  12. A matrix. Let \(\mat W_{\mathrm{C}}\) be the matrix with the entries \((\mat W_{\mathrm{C}})_{\mathrm{ij}} = g_{\mathrm{i}}(h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}})/h\). Let \(|\vek v| < \rho\). By lemma 1.21, \(\vek v = v_{\mathrm{x}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} + v_{\mathrm{y}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}} + v_{\mathrm{z}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\). The vectors \(v_{\mathrm{x}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(v_{\mathrm{y}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(v_{\mathrm{z}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) and \(v_{\mathrm{x}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} + v_{\mathrm{y}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) have the lengths \(|v_{\mathrm{x}}|\), \(|v_{\mathrm{y}}|\), \(|v_{\mathrm{z}}|\) and \(\sqrt{v_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + v_{\mathrm{y}}^2}\), which are not larger than \(|\vek v|\) (lemma 1.28) and are therefore smaller than \(\rho\). By step 10, used first for \(v_{\mathrm{x}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} + v_{\mathrm{y}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(v_{\mathrm{z}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\), then for \(v_{\mathrm{x}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(v_{\mathrm{y}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\vek g(\vek v) = \vek g(v_{\mathrm{x}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}) + \vek g(v_{\mathrm{y}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}) + \vek g(v_{\mathrm{z}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}})\). The vector \(v_{\mathrm{j}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\) is \((v_{\mathrm{j}}/h)\) times the vector \(h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\) and has the length \(|v_{\mathrm{j}}| < \rho\), so by step 11, \(\vek g(v_{\mathrm{j}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}) = (v_{\mathrm{j}}/h)\,\vek g(h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}})\). The component \(\ix{i}\) is
    \[g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek v) = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \frac{g_{\mathrm{i}}(h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}})}{h}\,v_{\mathrm{j}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} (\mat W_{\mathrm{C}})_{\mathrm{ij}}\,v_{\mathrm{j}} = (\mat W_{\mathrm{C}}\,\vek v)_{\mathrm{i}} .\]
  13. Antisymmetry. In (1.74) we put \(\vek v = h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(\vek w = h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\). The vector \(h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\) has only the component \(\ix{i}\) different from zero, and \(h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\) only the component \(\ix{j}\), so of the sum on the left only the term with the component \(\ix{i}\) remains, and of the sum on the right only the term with the component \(\ix{j}\). The left side is \(h\,g_{\mathrm{i}}(h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}) = h^2\,(\mat W_{\mathrm{C}})_{\mathrm{ij}}\), the right side \(-h\,g_{\mathrm{j}}(h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}) = -h^2\,(\mat W_{\mathrm{C}})_{\mathrm{ji}}\). So \((\mat W_{\mathrm{C}})_{\mathrm{ij}} = -(\mat W_{\mathrm{C}})_{\mathrm{ji}}\), and \(\mat W_{\mathrm{C}}\) is antisymmetric.
  14. The gradient near \(C\). By step 12, \(\vek u(X) = \vek u(C) + \mat W_{\mathrm{C}}\,\overrightarrow{CX}\) for every point \(X\) at a distance less than \(\rho\) from \(C\). Let \(X\) be at a distance less than \(\rho/4\) from \(C\). By lemma 1.89 on the neighbourhood of an interior point, all points at a distance less than \(\rho/4\) from \(X\) are at a distance less than \(\rho\) from \(C\). For \(0 < |\Delta| < \rho/4\) we therefore have, by lemma 1.97 on the linearity of the product with a matrix,
    \[\begin{aligned} u_{\mathrm{i}}(X + \Delta\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}) - u_{\mathrm{i}}(X) &= \big(\mat W_{\mathrm{C}}\,(\overrightarrow{CX} + \Delta\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}})\big)_{\mathrm{i}} - \big(\mat W_{\mathrm{C}}\,\overrightarrow{CX}\big)_{\mathrm{i}} \\ &= \Delta\,(\mat W_{\mathrm{C}})_{\mathrm{ij}} . \end{aligned}\]
    The difference quotient is \((\mat W_{\mathrm{C}})_{\mathrm{ij}}\) for every such \(\Delta\), so by lemma 1.26 on the limit of a number plus a multiple, \(H_{\mathrm{ij}}(X) = (\mat W_{\mathrm{C}})_{\mathrm{ij}}\). The displacement gradient equals \(\mat W_{\mathrm{C}}\) at all points at a distance less than \(\rho/4\) from \(C\).
  15. Zero derivatives of the gradient. By step 14 each function \(H_{\mathrm{ij}}\) is constant at all points at a distance less than \(\rho/4\) from \(C\). For \(0 < |\Delta| < \rho/4\) we therefore have \(\big(H_{\mathrm{ij}}(C + \Delta\,\vek e_{\mathrm{k}}) - H_{\mathrm{ij}}(C)\big)/\Delta = 0\), and the partial derivative \(\partial H_{\mathrm{ij}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}\) is zero at \(C\). We picked the point \(C\) arbitrarily, so each of the nine functions \(H_{\mathrm{ij}}\) has all partial derivatives equal to zero at every point of \(D\).
  16. A constant gradient. By lemma 1.133 on zero partial derivatives on a connected set, each function \(H_{\mathrm{ij}}\) is constant on \(D\). We choose a point \(C_0\) of \(D\) and write \(\mat W = \mat H(C_0)\). By step 14 at \(X = C_0\), \(\mat W = \mat W_{\mathrm{C}_0}\), which is antisymmetric by step 13. So \(\mat H(P) = \mat W\) for every point \(P\) of \(D\).
  17. A shift. Let \(f_{\mathrm{i}}(P) = u_{\mathrm{i}}(P) - \sum_{\mathrm{j}} W_{\mathrm{ij}}\,x_{\mathrm{j}}(P)\) for \(P\) in \(D\). The partial derivative of the sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} W_{\mathrm{ij}}\,x_{\mathrm{j}}\) with respect to \(x_{\mathrm{k}}\) is \(W_{\mathrm{ik}}\) (lemma 1.81), so \(\partial f_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{k}} = H_{\mathrm{ik}} - W_{\mathrm{ik}} = 0\) at every point of \(D\). By the same lemma on zero partial derivatives, each function \(f_{\mathrm{i}}\) is constant on \(D\). Let \(\vek a = (f_{\mathrm{x}}(C_0), f_{\mathrm{y}}(C_0), f_{\mathrm{z}}(C_0))\). Then \(u_{\mathrm{i}}(P) = f_{\mathrm{i}}(P) + \sum_{\mathrm{j}} W_{\mathrm{ij}}\,x_{\mathrm{j}}(P) = a_{\mathrm{i}} + \sum_{\mathrm{j}} W_{\mathrm{ij}}\,x_{\mathrm{j}}(P)\), so \(\vek u(P) = \vek a + \mat W\,\vek r_{\mathrm{P}}\) for every point \(P\) of \(D\).

2. The converse.

  1. The component \(\ix{i}\) of the field (1.72) is \(u_{\mathrm{i}}(P) = a_{\mathrm{i}} + \sum_{\mathrm{j}} W_{\mathrm{ij}}\,x_{\mathrm{j}}(P)\). The number \(a_{\mathrm{i}}\) has the derivative zero, and the coordinate \(x_{\mathrm{j}}\) has the derivative \(1\) with respect to \(x_{\mathrm{j}}\) and \(0\) with respect to the other coordinates (lemma 1.81). So \(\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} = W_{\mathrm{ij}}\) at every point, and the displacement gradient is \(\mat W\).
  2. The small strain tensor is \(\tfrac12(\mat W + \mat W^\T)\). Since \(\mat W^\T = -\mat W\), this is \(\tfrac12(\mat W - \mat W) = \mat 0\).

Source: SADD (2.2.9) and (2.2.10) (PDF pp. 44-45) writes the most general small rigid-body displacement with components and says for the plane form (2.2.9) that it gives zero strains. That with zero strains the displacements are at most such a motion, SADD states without proof (§6.2, PDF p. 133). CM (PDF p. 143) shows that a displacement with a constant antisymmetric matrix is a small rigid rotation. The proof is not from the sources.

The proof had three parts, as announced, and each has its part of the figure. In steps 1 to 4 the derivative along a segment, together with the corollary on a function with zero derivative, showed that no segment in the body gets longer to first order. In steps 5 to 13 the triangle in the ball turned this perpendicularity into linearity: the equality (1.74), which swaps the roles of two vectors at the cost of a sign, gave the sum, the multiple and the antisymmetric matrix. In steps 14 to 17 we passed from the ball to the whole set, by broken lines, just as for the bar we concluded from a zero derivative that a function is constant on an interval. The proof needs no second derivatives. We will meet the derivative along a segment again in chapter 4, where we will also use the theorem.

Let us test the theorem on the square plate of section 1.17.6. Lengths are measured in centimetres, the side of the plate is \(5\), and the corners are \(O = (0, 0, 0)\), \(A = (5, 0, 0)\), \(B = (5, 5, 0)\) and \(C = (0, 5, 0)\). Take \(\vek a = \vek 0\) and the antisymmetric matrix with a single pair of entries, \(W_{\mathrm{xy}} = -s\) and \(W_{\mathrm{yx}} = s\), with \(s = 0{,}001\). The field is \(\vek u = \mat W\,\vek r = (-s\,y,\ s\,x,\ 0)\). In micrometres the side of the plate is \(5\ \text{cm} = 50\,000\) µm, and the corner \(A\) moves by \(s \cdot 50\,000\ \text{µm} = 0{,}001 \cdot 50\,000\ \text{µm} = 50\) µm. The displacements of the corners are

\[\vek u(A) = (0, 50, 0) , \qquad \vek u(B) = (-50, 50, 0) , \qquad \vek u(C) = (-50, 0, 0) .\]

Let us draw this (figure 1.409), seen from above. The axis \(x\) points to the right, the axis \(y\) up. The blackwhite square is the plate \(OABC\) before the movement. The movement is greatly magnified in the figure: instead of \(s = 0{,}001\), \(s = 0{,}3\) is drawn, so that it can be seen. The orange quadrilateral is the plate after the movement with the field \(\mat W\,\vek r\), with the corners \(A_1\), \(B_1\) and \(C_1\). It stays a square: the orange right-angle marks show a right angle at all four corners. The corner \(O\) does not move. The blue dimensions are the displacements of the corners \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\). Each is perpendicular to the segment from \(O\) to this corner: for \(A\) and \(C\) this is a side of the plate, for \(B\) the grey diagonal, as the grey right-angle marks show. Each is also \(s\) times the length of this segment, in the figure \(0{,}3 \cdot 5 = 1{,}5\) cm for \(A\) and \(C\) and \(0{,}3 \cdot 5\sqrt2 \approx 2{,}1\) cm for \(B\). So the plate turns about \(O\), and for such a large \(s\) it also grows slightly. The grey dashed square is the exact rotation with the same \(s\). Its lengths do not change, while the orange side is slightly longer. The difference is a term with the square, at \(s = 0{,}3\) it is \(4{,}4\) %, at \(s = 0{,}001\) it is \(5{,}0 \cdot 10^{-7}\).

Let us also write the vectors of the segments in micrometres, so that both factors in the sum (1.73) are in the same unit. For the segment \(OB\) with \(\vek d = (50\,000, 50\,000, 0)\) µm the sum is \((-50) \cdot 50\,000 + 50 \cdot 50\,000 + 0 = 0\) µm², and for the segment \(AC\) with \(\vek d = (-50\,000, 50\,000, 0)\) µm it is \((-50 - 0) \cdot (-50\,000) + (0 - 50) \cdot 50\,000 = 0\) µm². Each corner moves perpendicular to its segment from \(O\) (figure 1.409). The lengths, though, change by a term with a square. The segment \(OA\) of \(50\,000\) µm becomes the segment to the point \((50\,000, 50, 0)\) with the length

\[\sqrt{50\,000^2 + 50^2}\ \text{µm} = 50\,000{,}025\ \text{µm} ,\]

which is \(5{,}0 \cdot 10^{-7}\) of the length more. This is \(s^2/2\). In general, for every vector of a segment \(\vek d\) the new vector is \(\vek d + \mat W\vek d\), and when we expand the square of its length as in section 1.17.5,

\[|\vek d + \mat W\vek d|^2 = |\vek d|^2 + 2\,\vek d^\T\mat W\vek d + |\mat W\vek d|^2 = |\vek d|^2 + |\mat W\vek d|^2 ,\]

because \(\vek d^\T\mat W\vek d = 0\) by corollary 1.104 on the double sum and the antisymmetric part, item 1. The exact rotation with the same \(s\) from section 1.17.6, which moves the corner \(A\) to \((5c, 5s, 0)\), differs from the field \(\mat W\vek r\) only by a term with a square: it moves the corner \(A\) by \(0{,}025\) µm less in the direction of the axis \(x\), since \(5 \cdot (1 - c) = 2{,}5 \cdot 10^{-6}\) cm. The exact rotation keeps the lengths and has \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = c - 1 = -5{,}0 \cdot 10^{-7}\), while the field \(\mat W\vek r\) has a zero small strain tensor and lengthens by \(5{,}0 \cdot 10^{-7}\). For steel structures, where we are interested in strains around \(0{,}001\), the two rigid motions are equally good.

The theorem gives the answer to the question at the start of the section.

Corollary 1.135 Two fields with equal strains (polji z enakimi deformacijami)

Let \(D\) be a connected open set of points (definition 1.130), and let \(\vek u\) and \(\tilde{\vek u}\) be displacement fields, continuously differentiable on \(D\), that have the same small strain tensor at every point of \(D\). Then there are a constant vector \(\vek a\) and a constant antisymmetric matrix \(\mat W\) such that

\[\tilde{\vek u}(P) = \vek u(P) + \vek a + \mat W\,\vek r_{\mathrm{P}} \qquad \text{for every point } P \text{ of } D .\]
Proof

We must show that the difference of the fields satisfies the assumptions of theorem 1.134, item 1.

  1. Let \(\vek v = \tilde{\vek u} - \vek u\). The partial derivative of a difference is the difference of the partial derivatives (lemma 1.81), and the difference of continuous functions is continuous (corollary 1.69, item 1), so \(\vek v\) is continuously differentiable on \(D\).
  2. Entry \(\ix{i}\ix{j}\) of the small strain tensor of \(\vek v\) is \(\tfrac12\big(\partial v_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} + \partial v_{\mathrm{j}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\big)\). By step 1 it is the difference of the same entries for \(\tilde{\vek u}\) and \(\vek u\), which are equal by assumption. So the tensor of \(\vek v\) is zero at every point of \(D\).
  3. By theorem 1.134, item 1, \(\vek v(P) = \vek a + \mat W\,\vek r_{\mathrm{P}}\) with a constant \(\vek a\) and a constant antisymmetric matrix \(\mat W\), which is the claim.

Source: SADD (PDF p. 54), BOWER (PDF p. 61), BARBER §9.1.1 (PDF p. 139), where the claim is stated without proof: by integrating the strains we get the displacements only up to a rigid-body motion. The proof from the theorem is not from the sources.

So the displacement is determined by the strains up to six numbers: the three components of the vector \(\vek a\) and the three entries \(W_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(W_{\mathrm{xz}}\), \(W_{\mathrm{yz}}\) above the diagonal of the matrix \(\mat W\), since the entries below the diagonal are their opposites and the diagonal holds zeros (lemma 1.103, item 3). Six numbers are fixed by six conditions.

Let us look at this on the hanging bar. The steel hanging bar hangs under its own weight and is fixed in the model only at the centre \(O\) of the top face (figure 1.89, left). Its interior points form a cylinder, which is connected, so every other continuously differentiable field with the same strains differs from the field (1.18) at the interior points by an addition \(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r\). The point \(O\) lies on the surface, but it is the limit of the interior points \((1/n, 0, 0)\) with \(n = 1, 2, \dots\), with the coordinates in metres. When both fields are continuously differentiable on an open set that contains the bar with its surface, the same relation therefore holds at \(O\) too, for the displacements and for their partial derivatives (lemma 1.68 on continuity through sequences of points and lemma 1.41 on the uniqueness of the limit of a sequence).

What conditions does the fixing at \(O\) prescribe? The addition has at every point the displacement \(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r_{\mathrm{P}}\) and the small rotation tensor \(\mat W\), as we computed at the start of the section. At the point \(O\), where \(\vek r_{\mathrm{O}} = \vek 0\), it moves the material by \(\vek a\) and turns it by \(\mat W\). A fixing that holds back only the displacement of the point \(O\) requires \(\vek a = \vek 0\) and leaves \(\mat W\) arbitrary. It therefore allows the whole bar to turn a little about \(O\), since a rotation does not change the strains, and the displacement of the bar would not be determined. For it to be determined, the fixing at \(O\) must prevent the turning of the material as well. CM prescribes such an idealized fixing: the displacement at \(O\) is zero and the material next to \(O\) does not turn (CM (7.3.16) and PDF p. 306). The field of the bar satisfies both conditions: \(\vek u(O) = \vek 0\), and the entries of its small rotation tensor are \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}} = -0{,}6\,a\,y\), \(\omega_{\mathrm{xz}} = -0{,}6\,a\,z\) and \(\omega_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0\), which are zero at \(y = z = 0\). An addition that does not spoil the conditions must have \(\vek a = \vek 0\) and \(\mat W = \mat 0\). The field of the bar is therefore the only field with these strains that satisfies the conditions. CM writes the second condition so that all partial derivatives of the displacement off the diagonal of the gradient are zero at \(O\), which for the bar, which has no shear strains at \(O\), means the same.

The theorem and the corollary only require the body to be connected, not to be free of holes. The ring is connected by lemma 1.131, so two displacement fields of the ring with the same strains are equal up to \(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r\), although the ring has a hole. For the two separate cubes of figure 1.402, though, the corollary does not hold, because the set is not connected. The corollary is about how many fields with given strains there are when there is one. Whether there is one is another question, and for the ring the answer will be different. We look at this in the next section.

1.18.5 Bodies with holes

Theorem 1.127 says that strains that come from a displacement field satisfy the compatibility equations. So the equations are a necessary condition: if they fail, there is no displacement field. But are they also a sufficient condition? Does a displacement field exist for every six functions that satisfy the equations? The answer depends on the shape of the body.

How would we find the displacement from the strains? We pick a point \(P\) and the displacement there, for example zero.
