We get the displacement at another point \(Q\) by walking from \(P\) to \(Q\) along some curve in the body and adding up the changes of the displacement over short steps. By theorem 1.88 on the change of a field over a short step, the change over a short step is almost exactly the sum of the products of the partial derivatives with the components of the step. The partial derivatives of the displacement are not only strains, though: they also contain the rotation of the material (definition 1.116). So the rotation too has to be obtained by adding up its changes along the path, and these changes are determined by derivatives of the strains (lemma 1.128 on derivatives of the rotation from derivatives of the strains, SADD (2.6.3)-(2.6.7), PDF p. 52). Exact adding up along a curve we meet only in section 3.5. But already now we can see where the compatibility equations enter this computation and why a hole spoils everything. Let us take a plane problem, where \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) depend only on \(x\) and \(y\) and \(u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\), and in it the rotation \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\) (figure 1.410).

  1. What the strains prescribe. By lemma 1.128 with \(\ix{i} = x\), \(\ix{j} = y\) and \(\ix{k} = x\) or \(\ix{k} = y\), the partial derivatives of the rotation must be
    \[\frac{\partial\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial x} = p , \quad p = \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial y} - \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial x} , \qquad \frac{\partial\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial y} = q , \quad q = \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial y} - \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}}{\partial x} .\]
    We know the functions \(p\) and \(q\) once we know the strains. We look for a function \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\) with these two partial derivatives.
  2. A small loop. We go around the rectangle in the body with the corner \(A = (x_{\mathrm{A}}, y_{\mathrm{A}})\) and sides \(s\) and \(t\) in the directions of the axes \(x\) and \(y\), counterclockwise. In the figure, in part (1), the loop is drawn as four blue arrows just inside the sides: at the bottom to the right, on the right upward, at the top to the left and on the left downward. Beside each is the estimate of the change on that side. There is a minus at the top and left sides, because we walk them in the direction opposite to the axis, so with a step of negative sign. We estimate the change of the rotation along each side as for a short step: by the value of the prescribed derivative at the middle of the side, multiplied by the length of the side and by the sign of the direction of walking. The sum of these estimates around the loop is
    \[Z(s, t) = p(M_1)\,s + q(M_2)\,t - p(M_3)\,s - q(M_4)\,t ,\]
    where \(M_1 = (x_{\mathrm{A}} + \tfrac s2, y_{\mathrm{A}})\) is the middle of the bottom side, \(M_2 = (x_{\mathrm{A}} + s, y_{\mathrm{A}} + \tfrac t2)\) of the right one, \(M_3 = (x_{\mathrm{A}} + \tfrac s2, y_{\mathrm{A}} + t)\) of the top one and \(M_4 = (x_{\mathrm{A}}, y_{\mathrm{A}} + \tfrac t2)\) of the left one.
  3. The mean value theorem. We chose the middles of the sides because then the points \(M_1\) and \(M_3\) lie on the same vertical segment, and the points \(M_4\) and \(M_2\) on the same horizontal one. We apply the mean value theorem 1.84 to \(p\) along the vertical segment and to \(q\) along the horizontal one, as in steps 3 and 4 of the proof of theorem 1.125. We get a point \(T_1\) between \(M_1\) and \(M_3\) and a point \(T_2\) between \(M_4\) and \(M_2\) such that \(p(M_3) - p(M_1) = t\,\partial p / \partial y\,(T_1)\) and \(q(M_2) - q(M_4) = s\,\partial q / \partial x\,(T_2)\). Therefore
    \[Z(s, t) = s\,t\,\Big(\frac{\partial q}{\partial x}(T_2) - \frac{\partial p}{\partial y}(T_1)\Big) .\]
    This is the same structure as for the double difference (1.66): the difference of values on opposite sides becomes a derivative at an intermediate point.
  4. The compatibility equation. We differentiate \(q\) with respect to \(x\) and \(p\) with respect to \(y\) (lemma 1.81), and the mixed derivatives of the component \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) are equal by theorem 1.125:
    \[\frac{\partial q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial p}{\partial y} = 2\,\frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial x\,\partial y} - \frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial y^2} - \frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}}{\partial x^2} .\]
    The right side is the right side of the first equation (1.68) minus its left side. So the first equation holds exactly when \(\partial q / \partial x = \partial p / \partial y\). This is the condition that, by theorem 1.125, every function \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\) whose partial derivatives \(p\) and \(q\) are continuously differentiable satisfies.
  5. What this means for the loop. If the first equation holds at every point, the bracket in step 3 equals \(\partial p / \partial y\,(T_2) - \partial p / \partial y\,(T_1)\). When we shrink the rectangle towards \(A\), \(T_1\) and \(T_2\) approach \(A\), and when \(\partial p / \partial y\) is continuous, the bracket approaches zero. The sum of the estimates around the loop is then small even compared with the area \(s\,t\) that the loop encloses. If the first equation does not hold at \(A\), however, the quotient \(Z(s, t)/(s\,t) = \partial q/\partial x\,(T_2) - \partial p/\partial y\,(T_1)\) approaches the difference \(\partial q/\partial x\,(A) - \partial p/\partial y\,(A)\), which by step 4 is not zero. Why then is there no function \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\)? Suppose it exists. When we go around the rectangle, we return to \(A\), so the sum of the true changes of \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\) along the four sides is zero. The estimate \(Z(s, t)\) differs from this sum by the error \(Z(s, t) - 0\), which we compute with the double difference \(g(s, t)\) of the function \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\) ((1.66)). The true changes on the bottom and top sides give together \(-g(s, t)\), the true changes on the right and left sides give \(g(s, t)\). Steps 4 to 7 of the proof of theorem 1.125, applied to \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\) with the partial derivatives \(p\) and \(q\), give points \(Q_1\) and \(Q_2\) in the rectangle such that \(g(s, t) = s\,t\,\partial q/\partial x\,(Q_1) = s\,t\,\partial p/\partial y\,(Q_2)\). With step 3 the error is therefore
    \[\begin{aligned} Z(s, t) - 0 &= \Big(-s\,t\,\frac{\partial p}{\partial y}(T_1) + g(s, t)\Big) + \Big(s\,t\,\frac{\partial q}{\partial x}(T_2) - g(s, t)\Big) \\ &= s\,t\,\Big(\frac{\partial p}{\partial y}(Q_2) - \frac{\partial p}{\partial y}(T_1)\Big) + s\,t\,\Big(\frac{\partial q}{\partial x}(T_2) - \frac{\partial q}{\partial x}(Q_1)\Big) . \end{aligned}\]
    When the strains have continuous second partial derivatives, the derivatives \(\partial p/\partial y\) and \(\partial q/\partial x\) are continuous at \(A\). For every error \(\eta > 0\) there is therefore a \(\delta > 0\) such that their values at the points at distance less than \(\delta\) from \(A\) differ from the values at \(A\) by less than \(\eta/4\). For \(s^2 + t^2 < \delta^2\) all four points \(T_1\), \(T_2\), \(Q_1\) and \(Q_2\) are such, since they lie in the rectangle (step 1 of the proof of theorem 1.125). By the triangle inequality (lemma 1.6) each bracket is then smaller in size than \(\eta/2\), so \(|Z(s, t)| < \eta\,s\,t\). The error of the estimate is therefore small even compared with the area \(s\,t\). For the same \(s\) and \(t\) the quotient \(Z(s, t)/(s\,t)\) differs from the difference \(\partial q/\partial x\,(A) - \partial p/\partial y\,(A)\) by less than \(\eta/4 + \eta/4 = \eta/2\). By the triangle inequality this difference is therefore smaller in size than \(\eta + \eta/2\) for every \(\eta > 0\), that is, than every positive number, and by lemma 1.34 on inequalities with all positive numbers it is zero. The first equation would therefore hold at \(A\). If it does not hold, the function \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\) does not exist. For the first strip with \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = k\,y^2\) we have \(p = 2k\,y\) and \(q = 0\), so \(\partial p/\partial y = 2k\) and \(\partial q/\partial x = 0\) at every point. Both brackets in the error are zero: if \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\) existed, the estimate would be exact, \(Z(s, t) = 0\). By step 3, however,
    \[Z(s, t) = s\,t\,(0 - 2k) = -2k\,s\,t ,\]
    for \(k = -10\ \text{m}^{-2}\) and \(s = t = 1\) mm is therefore \(-2 \cdot (-10\ \text{m}^{-2}) \cdot 10^{-6}\ \text{m}^2 = 2 \cdot 10^{-5}\). The estimate is \(-2k\) times the area of the loop, while the error would be zero. The estimate of the change of the rotation after going around a square with edge 1 mm is not zero, but the true change would have to be zero. The function \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\) therefore does not exist, and the pieces of the strip do not fit together.
  6. From the rotation to the displacement. When \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\) exists, we know all partial derivatives of the displacement, \(\partial u_{\mathrm{i}} / \partial x_{\mathrm{j}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} + \omega_{\mathrm{ij}}\), and we look for the displacement in the same way. The condition from step 4 is satisfied for it by itself. By lemma 1.128, item 2, we have \(\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{i}} / \partial x_{\mathrm{k}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} = \partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} / \partial x_{\mathrm{k}} + \partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ik}} / \partial x_{\mathrm{j}} - \partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jk}} / \partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\), and the right side does not change when we swap \(\ix{j}\) and \(\ix{k}\), because \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jk}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{kj}}\). So no new equation arises.
  7. From loops to paths. Let us also draw part (2) of the figure. The closed thick line is the boundary of a body without a hole, the point \(P\) is the start of the paths, the point \(Q\) the end. The paths go along the sides of a grid of small squares: the lower, blackwhite one first to the right and then upward, the upper, blue one first upward, then to the right and at the end downward to \(Q\). The grey squares between the paths lie in the body, and this is the only thing that we require of the two paths. The two thin blackwhite loops in two neighbouring squares show that we go around each counterclockwise. Let us add up the sums \(Z\) around the loops of all the squares between the paths. Every inner side is traversed by the neighbouring squares in opposite directions, so its estimates cancel. Only the sides of the two paths remain, and the sum is exactly the sum of the estimates along the lower path minus the sum along the upper one. By step 5 each term is small compared with the area of its square, so the difference of the two paths is small compared with the area between the paths, and on an ever finer grid it approaches zero. So we get the same rotation along both paths, and then by step 6 the same displacement.

Steps 1 to 6 are proved with the tools of this chapter. Step 7 is only a sketch: exactly, with true sums instead of estimates and for arbitrary paths, we prove it in chapter 4, section 4.7.9. The sketch says what BARBER states (PDF p. 46): if the path from \(P\) to \(Q\) can be turned into every other path between the same two points by small changes, we get the same displacement along all paths, and a displacement field exists. In space the rotation has three components, \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(\omega_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\omega_{\mathrm{yz}}\), and a loop can be placed in each of the three planes. The same computation as in steps 1 to 4 gives nine conditions, among which there are exactly six different equations (1.68). For \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\) the loops in the planes \(x\)-\(y\), \(x\)-\(z\) and \(y\)-\(z\) give the first, fourth and fifth equation, for \(\omega_{\mathrm{xz}}\) the fourth, third and sixth, for \(\omega_{\mathrm{yz}}\) the fifth, sixth and second (we checked the computation with SymPy).

Figure 1.411 compares two bodies. On the left is the body without a hole, the blackwhite closed line is its boundary. The blue closed curve lies in it. The two smaller grey dashed copies and the dot show that the curve gradually shrinks to a point without leaving the body. On the right is the ring, a body with a hole between the outer and the inner blackwhite circle, with the points \(P\) and \(Q\) on each side of the hole. The grey dashed circle around the hole is a closed curve that we cannot shrink to a point without leaving the ring. In a ring, however, the path above the hole cannot be turned into the path below it without passing through the hole, that is, outside the body (figure 1.411). Between the paths there is no grid of squares that would all lie in the body, because the hole lies in between, where the strains are not defined. Step 7 therefore does not hold there, and the displacement obtained along one path can differ from the displacement obtained along the other.

A body with a hole differs from a body without one also in the displacement, which is not necessarily a single-valued function of the point. Love describes a hollow cylinder (LOVE, PDF p. 240, figure 1.412), which we draw along the axis. In part (1) the blackwhite circles are the inner and outer edge of the cylinder, the point \(O\) is the axis. From the cylinder we cut out a narrow wedge between two planes through the axis, in grey in the figure, and greatly enlarged so that it can be seen. The blackwhite radial lines are the faces of the cut. In part (2) we bring the faces together and join them along the thick orange line. The orange circles are the cylinder after the joining, its shape is only illustrative. The grey dashed lines show where the faces were before the joining. After the joining the parts of the body pull and push on one another, although no external force acts on it. The points \(S_1\) and \(S_2\) on the opposite faces of the cut, in part (2) the grey dots at the positions of the faces before the joining, move to the same point \(S\) of the joint, each with its own displacement, and the displacements differ by the vector from \(S_1\) to \(S_2\) across the wedge. If we go along a path around the axis, we return to the same point, but the displacement on returning is not equal to the displacement at the start, because we went across the joint, where the material moved so that the two faces coincided (LOVE, PDF p. 240). The region with a hole is turned by a cut into a region without a hole, and the displacement may jump across the cut (LOVE, PDF p. 241).

From history

Let us draw a timeline. The axis shows years. That the displacement may fail to be a single-valued function of the point was first indicated by G. Weingarten in 1901. Two-dimensional bodies, such as a plane circular ring, were treated by A. Timpe in 1906. A more general theory was developed in a series of notes by Vito Volterra, who called such deformations distorsioni. Love calls them dislocations (dislokacije) (LOVE, PDF p. 240). Volterra published a comprehensive account in 1907 (LOVE, PDF p. 240, TIMO, PDF p. 345).

The property that separates a body without a hole, such as a solid cylinder, from a body with a hole, such as a ring, has its own name.

Let us draw the shrinking. On the left is the square of all points \((s, t)\) for \(s\) and \(t\) between \(0\) and \(1\), with the axes \(s\) and \(t\). We call the number \(t\) the time of the shrinking. The square has the end values written beside the axes. The bottom side is the curve \(\gamma\), blue, where \(t = 0\). The horizontal grey lines at \(t = 1/3\) and \(t = 2/3\) are intermediate positions of the curve. The top side at \(t = 1\) is mapped to a single point, which the label \(Z\) above it shows. The arrow \(H\) shows that the rule \(H\) maps the square to the body on the right. There the blackwhite closed line is the outline of the region \(D\). The blue curve is \(\gamma\) at time \(0\), the two grey curves inside it are the positions at times \(1/3\) and \(2/3\), and the point \(Z\) is the goal of the shrinking. The grey dashed line is the path of the point \(\gamma(0)\), which is the start and end of the curve: this point is the image of the left and at the same time of the right edge of the square, since \(H(0, t) = H(1, t)\).

Definition 1.136 Simply connected body (enostavno povezano telo)

Let \(D\) be a set of points of space.

  1. A closed curve (sklenjena krivulja) in \(D\) is a rule \(\gamma\) whose input is a number \(s\) from the interval \([0, 1]\) and whose output is a point \(\gamma(s)\) of \(D\), such that every coordinate of the point \(\gamma(s)\) is a continuous function of the number \(s\) on \([0, 1]\) (definition 1.58) and \(\gamma(0) = \gamma(1)\).
  2. A closed curve \(\gamma\) can be shrunk continuously to a point in \(D\) if there is a rule \(H\) whose input is a point \((s, t)\) of the square \([0, 1] \times [0, 1]\) and whose output is a point \(H(s, t)\) of \(D\), such that every coordinate of the point \(H(s, t)\) is a continuous function of the point \((s, t)\) of the square (definition 1.67, written for points of the plane), and such that \(H(s, 0) = \gamma(s)\) for every \(s\), \(H(s, 1)\) is the same point for all \(s\) and \(H(0, t) = H(1, t)\) for every \(t\).
  3. The set \(D\) is simply connected (enostavno povezana) if every closed curve in \(D\) can be shrunk continuously to a point in \(D\). A body is simply connected if the set of its interior points is simply connected. A set or a body that is not simply connected is multiply connected (večkratno povezana), like the ring.

Source: SADD §2.6 (PDF p. 53), KREYSZIG §10.2 (PDF p. 449), where the definition is given in words. The formulation with the rule \(H\) is not from these sources.

The definition writes precisely what we describe with a rubber band. A closed curve is a line that ends where it starts. The number \(s\) says where on the line we are: as \(s\) runs from \(0\) to \(1\), the point \(\gamma(s)\) runs along the whole line and returns to the starting point. Continuity of the coordinates means that the line has no jumps. The number \(t\) in the rule \(H\) is the time of the shrinking from figure 1.414. For every fixed \(t\) the rule \(s \mapsto H(s, t)\) is again a closed curve, since \(H(0, t) = H(1, t)\): this is the rubber band at time \(t\). All points \(H(s, t)\) lie in \(D\), so the rubber band does not leave the set while it shrinks. The coordinates are continuous functions of the point \((s, t)\), so the rubber band neither tears nor jumps, neither along the line nor in time. For a body we look at the interior points, because the strains and their derivatives are defined there. The definition is written for sets of points of space, and for sets in the plane it reads the same. LEBL2 (PDF p. 86) describes a simply connected domain as a connected open set in which every path between two points can be continuously deformed into every other path between the same two points, and KREYSZIG (PDF p. 449) writes the definition for domains. We require connectedness separately in the theorems (definition 1.130).

A cube, a cylinder and a ball are simply connected: we shrink a curve by moving each of its points at the same time along a segment towards one chosen point. We prove this precisely in chapter 4, section 4.7.8, for all bodies in which every point can be joined to a chosen point by a straight segment inside the body. A cylinder with a spherical cavity inside is simply connected too, because every curve around the cavity can be slid past it (SADD, PDF p. 53), and so is a thick spherical shell, the body between two spheres with a common centre (KREYSZIG, PDF p. 449). We prove both in the same section of chapter 4. A ring, however, is not simply connected, because a curve around the hole cannot be shrunk without passing through the hole (SADD, PDF p. 53, KREYSZIG, PDF p. 449). We prove this too in the same section, for the ring with radii 40 mm and 60 mm and any height, hence also for such a tube, which is only a tall ring. If we cut a ring, it becomes simply connected, which we prove there as well.

Theorem 1.137 Sufficiency of the compatibility equations (zadostnost enačb kompatibilnosti)

Let the set of interior points of a body be connected (definition 1.130) and simply connected, and let six functions \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\) be defined at the interior points of the body, with continuous partial derivatives of first and second order. If they satisfy the compatibility equations (1.68) at every interior point, they are compatible strains: there is a displacement field from which we get them by (1.63).

Source: SADD §2.6 (PDF pp. 52-53), CM §3.7.2 (PDF p. 151). We prove the theorem in full in chapter 4, section 4.7.9. SADD proves it by adding up changes of the displacement along a curve and with a theorem about such sums around closed curves (Stokes' theorem), without stating the smoothness requirements separately. Continuous derivatives up to second order are what his proof uses of the strains.

We prove the theorem in chapter 4, once we can add up small changes precisely (section 3.5). First, in section 4.7.7, we prove it for bodies in which every point can be joined to one chosen point by a straight segment that does not leave the body. The box, the cylinder and the ball are such bodies, the ring is not. Then, in section 4.7.9, we build paths from several segments that avoid the holes, and with simple connectedness we show that the result does not depend on the choice of the path. The books make this step with Stokes' theorem about sums around closed curves (SADD, PDF p. 53, KREYSZIG §10.2, Theorem 3, PDF p. 449), but we will manage with straight segments in small balls. The displacement is determined by the strains up to a rigid-body displacement: in a connected body two fields with the same strains differ only by a shift and a small rotation of the body as a whole, \(\vek a + \mat W\vek r\) (corollary 1.135 on two fields with equal strains, SADD, PDF p. 54). This agrees with what we saw in section 1.6: a rigid-body displacement does not change distances, so it does not change the strains.

Why the body has to be simply connected is shown by an example (figure 1.415). A thin ring with an inner radius of 40 mm and an outer radius of 60 mm, the ring of lemma 1.131 with a small height \(2c\), lies in the plane \(z = 0\), with its centre at the origin \(O\). Let us prescribe to it a strain that we describe in words. Every short fibre lying along the ring, that is, around the hole, is to shorten by a thousandth. Every short fibre pointing toward the centre is to keep its length. The right angles between these two kinds of fibres are to stay right. The example is not from a source, but it follows the idea of BARBER §2.2.1 (PDF pp. 47-48).

Let us draw the ring before the deformation (figure 1.415, left). The blackwhite circles with radii 40 mm and 60 mm are the inner and outer edge. Between them is one more circle, with radius 50 mm, and segments every \(45^\circ\) point toward the centre. At the place of the eighth segment, at \(0^\circ\), is the cut. We draw the circles and segments because the prescribed deformation speaks about fibres along circles and fibres toward the centre. The point \(O\) is the centre. We first cut the ring along a segment from the inner to the outer edge (figure 1.415, left). The cut ring is simply connected (the proof is in chapter 4, section 4.7.8). It takes the prescribed strain like this. Every circle around the centre keeps its radius, and its arc shortens by a thousandth, like a fan that we close a little. The segments pointing toward the centre only turn about the centre. Their length stays the same, and they stay perpendicular to the circles, since a radius is always perpendicular to its circle. So the cut ring takes the prescribed strain. How to write it in the coordinates \(x\) and \(y\), and that the cut ring has a displacement field whose small strain tensor is exactly the prescribed one, we show in chapter 4, section 4.7.9. The ends of the cut, though, move apart (figure 1.415, right). A circle of radius \(r\) has the circumference \(2\pi r\), so its arc shortens by \(0{,}001 \cdot 2\pi r\), and by that much the ends of the cut move apart on this circle. On the inner edge this is \(0{,}001 \cdot 2\pi \cdot 40\) mm \(= 0{,}251\) mm, on the outer edge \(0{,}001 \cdot 2\pi \cdot 60\) mm \(= 0{,}377\) mm. The gap is wider outside than inside, in proportion to the radius, so it has the shape of a wedge. One end of the cut is turned about the centre relative to the other.

In the middle of the figure the neighbourhood of the point \(S\) is enlarged. The small grey dashed circle just around \(S\) on the left and the large one in the middle show the same region, a circle with radius \(2{,}5\) mm. In the middle are the cut and the point \(S\) on it. The points \(S_{\mathrm{n}}^+\) are above the cut, the points \(S_{\mathrm{n}}^-\) below it, at the distance \(1/n\) mm from \(S\), for \(n = 1, 2, 3, 4\), with arrows toward \(S\), because we approach \(S\). On the right is the cut ring after the deformation, in orange, with the upper and lower end of the cut. The grey dimensions across the gap at the radii \(43\) and \(57\) mm show that the gap is wider outside. The blue dimension is the gap between the ends on the circle with radius \(50\) mm, to which the points just above the cut and just below it move. The shortening is greatly magnified: \(0{,}08\) instead of \(0{,}001\), so the gap in the drawing is about 25 mm instead of \(0{,}314\) mm.

Since the cut ring has a displacement field, by theorem 1.127 the prescribed strains satisfy the compatibility equations at every interior point of the cut ring. We could have made the cut anywhere, and the strain would be the same, so the equations hold at every point of the ring. Can the whole ring take these strains too? Let us show by contradiction that it cannot. We denote by \(\vek u\) the displacement field of the cut ring that opens the gap, and suppose that the whole ring also has a continuously differentiable displacement field \(\tilde{\vek u}\) with the prescribed strains.

  1. The cut ring is a part of the ring, so \(\tilde{\vek u}\) is defined at its points too. The cut ring is an open set (lemma 1.131), so the partial derivatives of \(\tilde{\vek u}\) at its points are the same whether we look at the whole ring or only at the cut one. The field \(\tilde{\vek u}\), looked at only at the points of the cut ring, is therefore a continuously differentiable displacement field of the cut ring with the same strains as \(\vek u\).
  2. The cut ring is connected (lemma 1.131). By corollary 1.135 on fields with equal strains there are therefore a constant vector \(\vek a\) and a constant antisymmetric matrix \(\mat W\) such that \(\tilde{\vek u}(P) = \vek u(P) + \vek a + \mat W\,\vek r_{\mathrm{P}}\) at every point \(P\) of the cut ring (SADD, PDF p. 54).
  3. Let us choose the point \(S = (50, 0, 0)\) on the cut, with lengths in millimetres (figure 1.415, enlarged in the middle). We approach it from above through the points \(S_{\mathrm{n}}^+ = (50, 1/n, 0)\) and from below through the points \(S_{\mathrm{n}}^- = (50, -1/n, 0)\), \(n = 1, 2, \dots\) All these points are in the cut ring, since their coordinate \(y\) is different from zero, and both sequences converge to \(S\), since their terms are at distance \(1/n\) from \(S\).
  4. The field \(\tilde{\vek u}\) is continuously differentiable on the ring, which contains \(S\) too, so it is continuous at \(S\) (lemma 1.91). By lemma 1.68 on continuity through sequences of points, \(\tilde{\vek u}(S_{\mathrm{n}}^+)\) and \(\tilde{\vek u}(S_{\mathrm{n}}^-)\) therefore approach the same vector \(\tilde{\vek u}(S)\). The components of the field \(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r\) are polynomials and are continuous (corollary 1.69), so \(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r\) too approaches the same vector \(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r_{\mathrm{S}}\) along both sequences.
  5. By step 2, \(\vek u = \tilde{\vek u} - \vek a - \mat W\,\vek r\) at the points of both sequences. By step 4 and lemma 1.60 on computing with limits of sequences, applied to each component, the difference \(\vek u(S_{\mathrm{n}}^+) - \vek u(S_{\mathrm{n}}^-)\) approaches \(\vek 0\).
  6. The field \(\vek u\) of the cut ring, however, jumps across the cut. The points just above the cut move together with the upper end of the cut, the points just below it with the lower one, and on the circle of radius \(50\) mm the ends move apart by \(0{,}001 \cdot 2\pi \cdot 50\) mm \(= 0{,}314\) mm. The difference \(\vek u(S_{\mathrm{n}}^+) - \vek u(S_{\mathrm{n}}^-)\) therefore approaches a vector of length \(0{,}314\) mm, not the vector \(\vek 0\). This contradicts step 5.

The field \(\vek a + \mat W\vek r\) that the corollary allows is continuous across the cut as well, so it does not change the difference between the displacements of the two ends of the cut, and the gap in figure 1.415 cannot close. The whole ring cannot take these strains, even though the compatibility equations hold at every one of its points.

If we cut such a ring, strained it and forced the ends of the cut together, the pieces would have to strain further so that the ends meet. Displacement fields with a jump across a cut are used for cracks and for dislocations, defects in the structure of metal crystals (SADD, PDF p. 54). For a body with a hole we add to the compatibility equations conditions that the ends of such a cut match. That the two ends of the cut of the ring can differ only by a rigid-body displacement, described by six numbers, three shifts and three rotations, we prove in chapter 4, section 4.7.9. There we also show that the whole ring has a displacement field exactly when this rigid-body displacement is zero. There we also say which properties of the ring the proof uses, so that it holds for every body with one hole and a cut with these properties. BARBER (PDF p. 48) says that the same holds for every hole and that every hole in a body therefore adds six conditions. SADD (PDF pp. 53-54) writes the same conditions with sums along a curve around the hole.

With this we have answered the question from the start of the section. The six strain components cannot be arbitrary, because they come from three displacement components. We found how they are related by differentiating them twice and using the theorem on the symmetry of mixed partial derivatives, which we proved with the mean value theorem used twice. On the strip with the prescribed \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = k\,y^2\) we saw that pieces with strains that do not satisfy the equations do not fit together. In a body without holes the equations are enough, and in the ring we saw that they are not. When a displacement field exists, the strains in a connected body determine it up to a shift and a small rotation. We showed this by treating every segment in the body as a rigid rod and then passing from a small ball to the whole body along broken lines. In chapter 2 we turn to the forces that strain a body.
